utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Deverell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Cayley, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General Deverell, do you have all the binders that you need, and do you have a copy of your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, yes I do. And I have my footnotes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, if could apply for admission into evidence of 65 ter 2D00632, which you will recall was the last document that we looked at as we broke on Friday. It was the NATO definition of a military governor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Hedaraly has no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1787.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could, please, is it possible, Mr. Registrar, to look at -- it is. It has come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please move on, General Deverell, in your report, and if you could turn to page 51 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could have Exhibit D409.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And here, General Deverell, I'm interested in lines 22 to 37 of page 51. And, in particular, the reference to D409. Do you recognise this document, General Deverell?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing on my screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, [Microphone not activated] my computer is all down, nothing's down -- the screen is not working. And so I have no communications at all at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll seek the assistance of our technical experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, someone will look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Someone is here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we continue meanwhile. Mr. Misetic you have -- you could share, perhaps, with Mr. Kehoe. Yes, then we'll continue, because with the witness, I do understand that we're now okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Deverell, do you see that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you refer to this in your report at page 51?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please turn to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see, General Deverell, at the bottom there's a meeting at 1730 hours which was a meeting in the minister's office of Mr. Susak, Mr. Jarnjak, and Mr. Moric. Do you recall referring to this and reading this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you give the Court your comments that you made in respect of the document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It struck me that two things: Firstly, that quite clearly in my mind there was no discussion in the -- at the first meeting of -- what you might call post-conflict operations and that that was discussed or at least touched upon in this meeting at 1730 in the minister's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by post-conflict operations?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the management of the result of the operation you were conducting, you know, what happened, how -- how authority was -- was regained, and how order, civilian order, normal civilian life was re-established, the rule of law, et cetera, after the operation had been successfully conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now you note in your report at page 51 that you were -- I'll read to you exactly what you say. You say that: "Colonel-General Cermak went present at the meeting. This would have been a strange omission if it had intended that Colonel-General Cermak was to oversee on behalf of the president or the chief of the Main Staff the post-operational phase."

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason I said that is that in order to have any idea how you might conduct --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, I'm sorry, as I said to you last week, because we're speaking the language we have to make sure that we're going at a deliberate pace and make sure we pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I -- the reason I made that comment was that I don't think that you can be in a position to be responsible for overseeing post-conflict operations unless you understand the plan for the conflict, so to speak, how -- how one side was going do achieve its objective. And therefore I would have expected somebody who was going to do that job, going do oversee post-conflict resolution, or the post-conflict phase, I'm sorry, the post-conflict phase, actually at a meeting which discussed the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please move on and slightly changing topics. If we could look at D281.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you refer to this on page 19 of your report. Do you recognise this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could, first of all, go to page 9 of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And here, General, I'm interested in lines 28 to 34 of your report on page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could please move down to paragraphs 5.4 and 5.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if could you just briefly read those over, Mr. Deverell, then I will have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen those. I'm happy I know what those mean. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what I'm, in particular, interested in is the fact in -- in paragraph 5.4 it states that the reserve battalion shall be stationed in Knin barracks. And then in 5.5, it states again that the reserve company there of the HV 4th Guards Brigade shall be stationed in Knin southern barracks. Now, you were discussing with us last week about the duties of the garrison commander. Now, was this document sent to the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think if we look at the distribution list it was not sent to the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what is your comment about that, based on the fact that these units were being placed within garrison facilities in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite surprised that the garrison commander was not made aware, at least made aware that they were going to be there. And indeed in other armies it would have been his responsibility to have allocated the resources, the garrison resources, and not the operational commander to dictate who went where. But that is -- that is a matter of detail. The fact was he was not informed, not warned, that such a deployment was going take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go the last page of this particular document. And if -- is it possible to -- it is very very small. If that could be -- yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you make some observations about this organisational chart of the Split Military District as of 9th August, 1995. Can you -- can you tell the Court your comments about this document.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a perfectly normal what we would call an organisation of battle, and ORBAT, which tells everybody who -- what constitutes the force for which those orders have been prepared. It -- it is entirely back to the point that the commander must know who he has under his command and those under his command know that they are commanded by him or -- what organisation they lie within. And therefore who has the authority. What didn't surprise me particularly but is clearly not there is Knin garrison. And, therefore, I would deduce that they were not part of the operational order of battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And lastly if we can look at D774 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If -- if I could just seek clarification. If it is inappropriate, I can do it in cross-examination. I was confused whether the question related to the Split Military District as of 9 August; I see this is the Knin forward command post of the Split Military District. I just wanted to clarify, although I'm happy to do it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that would be fine in cross-examination, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could look at D774.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Judges what it is.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a communication plan, Your Honour. And all operations will have a communication plan so that people know not only how they communicate, things like radio frequencies, et cetera, but they also know the nicknames and code words such as may be required. And it -- it happens -- it is attached, it is part of -- an integral part of any operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, it's a lengthy document. I'm not going to go through page by page. But in your report you noted that Knin garrison was not part of this communications plan. Can you make your comments about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're not part of the communications plan, then there's no way that you can receive information. There's no way -- therefore you can analyse, decide, plan, and there's no way can you play any part that that operation, because have you no way of imparting your ideas or such plans as you may have. Without communications, you cannot be seen part of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what is the significance of the fact that Knin garrison is not within this communications plan?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not part of the operation element of Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move on, please, to part 12 of your report, which is dealing with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could have D267 brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is an order, General, of the 2nd of August, from Major-General Lausic to a number of military police battalions that can you see there. Have you -- you've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could go to page 4, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm interested, General, in the second paragraph of that particular complete paragraph 10 where it starts: "I appoint Major Ivan Juric ..." and it continues to the end of the paragraph stating that the commanders of the 72nd VP Battalion and 73rd VP Battalion should be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric. What were your comments about that part of that document, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- this is my comments. I think, well, this was very unusual because you had here a group of officers with Major Juric in charge of them placed in command of in that 72 and 73 were subordinated to Major Juric and this is -- this is unusual because the -- it broke the normal chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, again, the last three lines of the first full sentence that can you see on that page: "Commanders of the 72nd Battalion and 73rd VP Battalion to Major Ivan Djuric who shall report to the VP administration until 2000 hours every day starting from 4 August 1995." What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shows that those commanders had an obligation to report to Major Juric who reported direct to General Lausic. I used the -- I have subsequently used the phrase that Major Juric was his - and it's a military phrase - directed telescope. There was some confusion, Your Honour, with -- within the responsibilities for military police operations. The orders, in my opinion, were somewhat ambiguous and, indeed, at one stage had to be clarified. And I think that was an effect the -- the way that General Lausic attempted to ensure that there was proper control of the military police down the line the of military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have P879, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated the 5th of August. And it's a report by Major Juric. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could please turn to page 2, paragraph 1.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is, as can you see, Major Juric reporting that a military police company has been established in Knin with military policemen coming from the 72nd Military Police Battalion and the 66th Military Police Battalion. What comment do you have about this?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a -- quite clearly a combined unit, and it was Major Juric reporting directly that it had been formed, and its tasks, supervising patrol placed at the town entrance and exit, et cetera, et cetera. And this was part of his reporting obligation back to Major-General Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just to remind you before we move on to the next documents of the allegations in the indictment, and you will recall I read it out to you last week, I'm not going to read it out all again, but I will read to you one part of it where it alleges that Mr. Cermak possessed effective control over ... and then it lists a whole series of units. And then it says "a combined military police company consisting of elements or units from the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions." Now, ignoring the 73rd aspect, because I think that is a mistake in the indictment - I don't know if my learned friend can correct me if I'm wrong - but now I want to specifically address that issue with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could have D789 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, are you ... sorry, did you want to --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, I'm -- I'm fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just explain what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an instruction to carry out the rotation of the military police forces in Knin and gives details of who is in command, who is -- who are the platoon commanders, et cetera, and when this is to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I could just seek my learned friend's assistant, could you please guide me where D789 is referred to in Mr. Deverell' report? I'm sorry, I can't seem to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could wait until the break, and then I'll inform you, because I can't find it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Hedaraly wants to look at the context of where we find the report. Oh, this document addressed, so therefore it would not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can. It is, in fact, it's footnote 174, and it refers to three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you see to whom that document is delivered. Do you have any comments about the addressees on that document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does not include Knin garrison headquarters, in general, or General Cermak in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what does that indicate to you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It demonstrates two things. Firstly, that he had no authority over it, otherwise he would have been told; and secondly, it also demonstrates that they didn't -- were not particularly interested in telling General Cermak when they were changing over, which does strike me as being, as it were, strange, because you would have thought that if General Cermak had had any responsibility, authority, then he would have needed to know when that change-over was taking place, because change-overs affect the capacity of a unit to conduct their operations. There is quite clearly an administrative pause. So I would have expected, had he had any responsibility at all, for him to be have been informed that it was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now, please, look at D791, which is referred to on page 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see that it is a report by the commander of the Independent Knin Company about duties that were carried out on the 19th of August in Knin. And you can see the addressees in the top right-hand corner, the military police administration, general military police section.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, yes, I do. Once again, it demonstrates to me that General Cermak had no responsibility for the military police because it -- it talks about something they did without informing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could have D770.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I will give you the reference in a moment, Mr. Hedaraly. It's on page 41. General, if you need to refer to your footnotes, you can put them in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fine. I'm very happy there, thank you. If I dive out of the way, Your Honour, it's because I'm looking at my footnotes, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? And I will get to the subject matter, but if you just look at the header sheet.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is an order, as you can see, to hand over the protection of the General Cermak to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's sent directly to the military police, 66th Battalion. And on the front page, you will have noticed it was sent for information to Mr. Cermak. Can you make some comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, an information copies is a matter of -- I mean, firstly, in some ways, courtesy, and secondly, to inform him that something will happen that he may have an interest in, but he has to take no action. And it, once again, reflects to me that he is not part of the decision-making process in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now, please, turn to D788, which is on page 42 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What comments do you have about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given that General Cermak had no authority with the military police, which we've seen demonstrated, because Major Lausic was given the -- was the superior officer to the Knin military police company, because they were subordinated to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said Major Lausic there; did you mean Juric?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant -- I do apologise. Major Juric. General Cermak had no authority to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you do make some comments on why this order you believe was issued in respect of the preambulary paragraph which talks about establishing order and discipline between the Croatian army and UNCRO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I mean, I believe, from reading the -- the -- or looking at the context, that General Cermak, who had been in Knin two days - and we must remember that he had had almost no preparation time for this and had no experience in dealing with these matters - was in fact meeting a demand that had been identified to him through his -- his discussions and -- and what people had been telling him. He clearly thought or somebody had asked him to make sure that there was a control at the entrances to the UNCRO barracks, and he -- as part of his coordination and cooperation requirement as a garrison commander, although I guess he didn't realise he had it, I think he felt that he had to do something. He demonstrated -- he had to demonstrate that he was going do something, and, indeed, he wanted to achieve the -- the control of those entrances to the barracks. And he issued an order, but he no authority so to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence as to whether or not this order was ever carried out?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no evidence that the order was carried out at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at D303 which also on page 42 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What comments can you make about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very similar comment. I know that Brigadier-General Forand was pressing General Cermak in his meetings to do something about the equipment that had been stolen. Again, I think this is an example of General Cermak attempting to be helpful and to assist UNCRO who, after all, were then trying to -- to reduce their commitment in line with the agreement. And, again, he issues an order really trying to demonstrate that he was doing something but not being aware that he no authority to give that order and there was no authority to issue that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could I seek some clarification on one of the previous answers. Mr. Deverell, I'll just read to you how it was -- how it appears on the transcript. You said: "He clearly thought or somebody had asked him to make sure that there was a control at the entrance of the UNCRO barracks and he, as part of his coordination and cooperation requirement as a garrison commander, although I guess he didn't realise he had it, I think he felt he had to do something." Now, what didn't he realise that he had it, because that, at least, I can't understand that fully from this sentence, what he realised he didn't have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I didn't articulate that very well. One of the problems I think we have here is that General Cermak, who had been put into this job, as I've said we've discussed extensively, without any real time to prepare and without any of the experience that was required and without a substantial staff to give him guidance, would have been, I would suggest - and my deduction is that he would have been lacking in understanding as to exactly what powers he had and what powers he didn't have. There is this element of command and -- I'm sorry, coordination and cooperation which a garrison commander is supposed to conduct with other organisations which we have referred to. I was merely trying to, rather, inarticulately to draw attention to this -- this conflict. I do not believe he understood the limits of his authority. And that is the main reason why he wrote that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you intended to say is that you guessed that he didn't realise that he had no authority, although he was aware of his coordinating role, coordination and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a coordination and cooperation role. I do not think -- I would suggest he was not aware of that and he certainly was not aware -- was not aware of the authority that he had, and didn't realise -- I'm sorry, this is rather complicated. He did not realise how little authority he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So should I then understand your answer to be that he wasn't aware that his role was limited to coordination and cooperation, rather than having the authority to issue the kind of orders he issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is it a fair assessment, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could -- if we could please look at D503.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you've seen this document before. This is on page 42 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have seen it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could just go to the second page so that you can see all of the document. What do you have to say about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly the same as I've said about the first two. This is an example of General Cermak responding to a situation that was being explained to him, given to him by UNCRO, attempting to help UNCRO find these vehicles, to get their property back. He actually writes to both commanders of the military police and the civil police and says that they shall be answerable to him, when he no authority so to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could look at D304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, this all appears in the report, and to say that it should be highlighted because it might fail to have our attention, well, that -- a lot of attention has been given to these orders and the authority to issue these orders. I think at least five, six, or seven witnesses have given their views, and the report is quite clear on that. So I wonder why it has to be highlighted again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm actually coming to the end of this now, Your Honour. I'm -- I'm not going show any more orders. I'm just going to show two letters, and then I'll finish with it and move on to another subject. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should have asked it that way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you have seen this before too?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just be allowed to read it onto the second page. Can you explain what deductions you drew from this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, that, as he clearly says, he's had no -- there has been no success in finding these vehicles. And, secondly, he does what perhaps he should have done from the start, realised that it is the chain of command, it is the operational command, who really has the responsibility down the chain of command through the brigades and to the battalions to find these vehicles. They have the manpower, they also have the military police support, and he is really now beginning to learn, I deduce, that this is the way he should have done things, because it is General Gotovina who is able to issue the proper instructions that these pieces of equipment should be looked for and, if found, handed back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And without looking at that document, you've actually seen that and referred to in your report --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- the letter that General Gotovina writes to other units in the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I have, yeah, as a result of this. And I would say that that was the proper way of doing it, the effective way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's D305. If we could now turn to part 13 of your report. And this is the part entitled "Ivan Cermak and the Civilian Authorities in Knin." And, again, these are -- the documents that are referred to here are documents that the Court has seen, so I'm not going to go through all of them. But let's look at a few and then you can certainly give your comments to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have D298.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is on page 49 of your report. What comments, if any, do you have about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that there was a requirement, and one of the main reasons that General Cermak was sent to this area was to help with the -- as have I referred to it, the urban regeneration of Knin. And this is an example of him doing just that. It demonstrates that he needs the assistance of UNCRO to help him do this, and there is some discussion about this in a series of reports. And this is -- this is a sign of him carrying out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And we'll skip the next document but go to D1125, which is also on page 49. You've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what comments do you make about this?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is an attempt by him to -- a successful attempt, I believe, to ensure that there is the proper access to fuel for both the Croatian army and I would suggest, in general terms, to the civil population and is part of his urban regeneration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And let's -- you've referred to quite a few documents here, but let's look at one more, which is D1120, page 49 of the report. You've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen an order to a bank before, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I haven't actually seen an order to a petrol station either, as it so happens. But I have not seen an order to a bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what comments, if any, do you have about this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first comment is, of course, again, it's a continuation of the urban regeneration. I have no idea why it was written as an order. I have seen nothing in my reading of all the documents that appears to give him the -- the authority to write an order to a bank. But he was a businessman; it may have been this was the final act in a series of conversations which he will. I mean, I deduce that this was so and that he decided to finalise it, to put a stamp of authority on it by calling it an order. But I -- I would doubt whether it had any status as an order. If we could now, lastly, go to part 14 of your report. And here I just really just have a few questions about this. This is Ivan Cermak and international organisations in Knin. Now, you said on Friday that you yourself had had some experience of dealing with international organisations in Bosnia. Can you just remind us very briefly of what you said?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I -- the points I was trying to make was that international organisations had a sort of a dynamic of their own, Your Honour. Having been a member of one, you tend to look for the most senior officer you can find, the most senior person you can find, because he, as far as you are concerned, will the person who can deliver what you want and also be able to coordinate and cooperate with you. One thing you must do as an international organisation is know that you have made the right choice, and you really have to look behind the person to see what network what he has, what network he's using, what staff he has, whether he has a properly constructed staff. And if he hasn't or she hasn't, then possibly you're using -- you're going to the wrong person. And that is -- that is a particular important area. The second area, if this is what Mr. Cayley's referring to, is the choice of a point of contact. A point of contact should really be a facilitator, a person who does not have direct authority, a go-between, a conduit of information who can bring people together in order to reach agreements that have probably been previously decided. In my experience, it's not helpful to have a point of contact who is themselves are themselves commanders because they carry too much responsibility; they're not able to negotiate. Negotiation is a very important part of this. They're not able to negotiate as easily as somebody who does not have that authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In Bosnia, what was the rank and position of your specific point of contact?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point of contact that we had, that is, the -- the NATO force, with the entity armed forces the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and the Federation was actually a brigadier. He did not have any command responsibilities at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've said at the beginning of part 14 that of the three tasks that he, referring to Mr. Cermak, was given, the most complex and sensitive was to be the point of contact for international organisations. Why do say that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international organisations themselves are very complicated; they have very sensitive agendas. Often you're dealing with organisations that have very different agendas. And you are particularly exposed because they are reporting back to international -- international -- sorry, headquarters in international -- I will say that again. They are reporting back to international headquarters in other cities. Also, they -- they have a very close relationship with the press or perhaps the press has a very close relationship with them. And, therefore, what you say is often directly reproduced on the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Kehoe, are you the next in line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Gladly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Deverell, will you now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'm -- if you can bear with me I'm just going to jump around in your report on a few things. And if it seems a bit confusing, I'm certainly not going to go through the recitation that Mr. Cayley went through. So if you can bear with me on that score. Now, in a couple of issues that you referred to and the first I would like to talk to you about is the general receipt of information. Several times during the course of your report, and I believe in discussions with Mr. Cayley you talked about General Cermak as a recipient for information only for which he did not have to take any actions. And, you know, the case in point that I believe you cite is P918.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up. It is the Mario Tomasovic document. It will come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For ease of reference, I believe this is mentioned on page 39 of your report, General. And it is a document that is well known to the Chamber that comes from the the assistant commander for political affairs for the Split Military District, and it goes to assistant commanders for political affairs. An outlines various items, beware -- make sure looting and burning and theft doesn't take place, that the second paragraph the President Tudjman and the country has condemned such activities. And on the next page is where you note that it is to the Knin garrison for information. And if we go three lines up, it is also for General Gotovina as the commander of the Split Military District for information. Now, General, based on the research that you have -- you know - do you not? - that this was part of a series of orders and moves by at least General Gotovina to condemn crime and to put his subordinate commanders on notice that they have to go out and stop any undisciplined activity. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And so when you went through this - and I know you went through, for instance, if we can turn to -- if I can just mention it, it's P71 - where, on the 9th of -- and this is in the Split Military District diary, General Gotovina says that the military police is to take security control, war-booty, and take photographs, and make video recordings at the end of the operation. People will be called before military disciplinary court. And just prior to this -- this order, or this document that you cited by -- in D918, we have D204.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just referred you to an oral order, but, I believe, this is the hard copy order that you referenced, D204, General Gotovina's order of the 10th, two days prior to Captain Tomasevic's notice. And there was sequence in pattern to these, was there not, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you assess that the command of the Split Military District was making attempts to stop any ill-disciplined activity?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, General, if I pause I'm waiting for the translators to catch up so ... Now, the next issue I would like to -- to address is the military police which Mr. Cayley touched on very briefly. And on pages 20 and 21 of your report you note that that the military police have their own chain of command. But I'm more interested in -- in the comments that you make on page 46 and 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to that. And that's in D1084, page 46 and 47. I believe that's the exhibit number for the report. My learned friend Mr. Cayley may be able to help me. I believe it is D284 -- excuse me, 1084.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in this -- this assignment of Major Juric to Knin, and I believe you referred to it as a telescope, that he sent his men to Knin. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the word "directed telescope," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The directed telescope?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direct the telescope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during the course of your discussion with Mr. Cayley, we went through some documents between Mr. Juric and Mr. Lausic, and Mr. -- Colonel Budimir and Mr. Lausic and Mr. Juric, and when we looked at that documentation, we saw Juric filing reports directly to Mate Lausic, General Mate Lausic, and also -- you also commented that those reports were not sent to General Cermak. But they were also not sent to General Gotovina either, were they?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, and you talk about this on page 44 of your report, if we can just discuss the rationale of having the military police independently investigate crime, which I take from your report at 44 is, in fact, the situation not only in the HV but likewise the situation in the -- armed forces of the United Kingdom. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Give us the rationale for having a -- an independent military police investigating crime - and when I say "independent," independent of the command structure - that they may be in the same geographical area with?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it's quite simple, really. It's important to have your criminal investigation capability independent of the chain of command because it might at some stage be investigating the chain of command. The chain of command might have -- might feel that they do not want a proper investigation conducted. And, therefore, there is a great advantage in having those two separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is it clear from the documentation that you examined, General, that Mate Lausic took very significant steps to ensure that the military police and him personally stayed in control of those investigations by requiring that daily reporting from Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- very careful separation. And, indeed, the -- there were instructions that brigades or the operational chain of command only had a cooperation and coordination relationship with the military police over what were called regular police tasks. And they are relatively limited ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned during the course of your report that the comment "regular police tasks" isn't defined. But based on your analysis of common police tasks, investigating crime is not one of those common police tasks, and investigating crime is something that was in the individual domain of the -- the sole domain of the military police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is as I would expect to see it, and that is as I found it when reading the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not objecting, but I'm just noticing, Mr. President, there's - and I don't think it's anybody's fault - we're talking about regular police tasks then Mr. Kehoe talks about common police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I meant "regular." I stand corrected, Mr. Cayley, thank you. I meant regular police tasks which is, I believe, the correct terminology. I appreciate that, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could just move to another subject, and this also touches upon a document that Mr. Cayley addressed with you this morning which had to do with the planning for post-conflict operations. And if I could read for you what you said just this morning. And this would be, I believe, page 4, lines 13 to 19. And, General, if I'll read this slowly, and it says: "The reason I -- the reason I made that comment was that I don't think that you can be in a position to be responsible for overseeing post-conflict operations unless you understand the plan for the conflict, so to speak, how one side was going do achieve its objective. And therefore, I would have expected somebody who was going to do that job, going do oversee post-conflict" -- it's -- the terminology is -- I think we have a mistake there, but it says "phase, actually at the meeting." Essential what you were saying was that if General Cermak was going to be responsible for the post-conflict resolution, he would have been at the post-conflict resolution meetings. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the document that we were talking about on that score was D409, I believe, Mr. Cayley discussed that with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could just bring that up. D409.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I, while we're waiting, could clarify something, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only do I believe that anybody responsible for post-conflict, the post-conflict phase should have been at the post-conflict phase meeting, they should have also been at the meeting which discussed the plan of how to get to the post-conflict phase. Namely, the operational planning meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. And let's just go through that just briefly. And I do believe that in your report, again, at page 51, you discuss this meeting and General Cermak's participation or lack thereof. And in talking about this, you note that this would have been a strange omission. This is page 51, line 26. This would have been a strange omission if it had been intended that General Cermak was to oversee on behalf of the president or the chief of the Main Staff, the post-operational phase. Now, if we look at the document that's before us, this is a multi-page document that has, in fact, two meetings. The 10.00 meeting at which General Gotovina is present is the, as you know, an operational meeting to discuss the plans for Operation Storm. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe we -- if we just turn to, for instance, page 3, we have Admiral Domazet talking about the numbers of possible men. And this is for the entire Operation Storm, not just Sector South. Minister Susak talking about the amount of troops that are mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then if we can go to page -- two more pages up, page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now there is this -- there is the meeting at 1730 on the same day, General, where Minister Susak, from the Ministry of Defence, Minister Jarnjak for the Ministry of the Interior, and the assistant minister of the interior, Josko Moric is present, and there is no General Cermak, and there's no General Gotovina either. Now, expanding from your comment in your expert report, if, in fact, someone like General Gotovina was going to be responsible for post-operational resolution, if you will, you would have expected him at this meeting as well, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when we were talking about a post-operational phase, again, if you're going to responsible for it, you have to be part of the planning ahead of time, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it was clear - was it not, General? - that this -- and I believe you touched upon this just briefly with Mr. Cayley when talking about the military governor issue and the fact that military governor -- only being a term of international -- only is involved in occupied territory, i.e., a different country other than your own?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it was clear on this that the idea from the beginning was that once the HV took the ground in the Krajina that the civilian authorities would say immediately come in and take over and restore constitutional order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think that -- I do believe that you reviewed D1634, which is a presidential transcript of 4 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just go to that front sheet, D1634. And if we could turn to page 7 in the English, comments of Minister Jarnjak. If I can just check to see what it is in the Croatian. I think that's at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Minister Jarnjak of the Ministry of Interior notes that: "Mr. Prime Minister, alongside participating in this combat segment, what the defence minister was talking about in agreement with the very -- with the minister of defence, we have prepared 3.500 policemen in regular blue uniforms from the north-west and northern part of Croatia, a part which is not directly participating in the war. 500 of them have already been sent to Zadar, Gospic, and Sibenik because as the army enters the area, the military police follows which secures the line and, immediately after, the regular police enters the area and takes over all those tasks. The regular police is obligated to conduct, according to the constitution and the law, and those are maintaining public peace and order, protection of life and property." Now, consistent with -- that clearly is consistent with the meeting that takes place on the 2nd; is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That the army is going to go in, the military police follows, then immediately the civilian police come over and restore constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the idea from your reading of these documents was that the HV -- the army itself would move on to other tasks. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could move back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we may just -- just so that the record is clear, I think that Mr. Kehoe referred to D1634 as a presidential transcript. It's a transcript of an a closed session of the government meeting. Just so there is no confusion later on. There is no issue. I think Mr. Kehoe will see that but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I do believe you're 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could just flip back to D409. General, this the was the document we were talking about previously, the 2 August 1995 meeting where there were discussions about Storm. And it's clear, during this, that General Gotovina is an operational commander about to engage in a substantial military operation in the area. And based on your career, General, and your unique position, not only within the United Kingdom, but throughout the western world, I mean, tell us a little bit, General, if you will, about the duties and the responsibilities of an operational commander. I mean, what's on his mind, what's going on when an operational commander is conducting combat operations both before, during, and after?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before it is quite clearly the planning phase, and, indeed, the planning phase is possibly demanding -- because it requires the greatest intellectual conceptual effort, that is where the idea is created. It is not half as time-consuming and the coordination phase. Once the orders have been given, are things in the right place, is the -- does the plan stand up to the realities of the logistic -- the logistic requirements and so on and so forth, is the intelligence still supporting the basic thrust of your plan. So the commander is absolutely focussed, depending on how complex the plan is and how large the organisation is, is absolutely focussed on that plan and the implementation of that plan. And once you have gone into your -- you've started conducting your plan, then whatever work you were doing beforehand is doubled. Because you have to monitor, analyse, continue to decide, and we have a thing called planning which is a continuous activity. This may sound obvious, and I apologise if it does, but often people believe that you have plan and you merely go through the steps rather like playing a board game. My experience is that once you actually confront the reality, then your planning activity becoming more frenetic and more demanding. So the commander is absolutely focussed, and he does not have time to deal with other matters, and has to prioritise very profoundly at times on what he is to concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you know based on your overall knowledge of this sequence of events, not only with Operation Storm, but that after Operation Storm -- pardon me, Operation Storm was preceded by several combat actions in Bosnia, Operation Storm then took place. General Gotovina set up the active defence order that you were looking at this morning, and then you also note that the HV, in conjunction with other armies, the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, embarked on additional offensive operations against the VRS in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You know that based on --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- your knowledge coming to this Court. Now, General let's take that and talk about the focus of an operational commander moving into Operational Storm; getting read for an active defence; resupplying, replenishing his troops; moving onto the line; and moving forward. I mean, what kind of focus and what kind of energy does and operational commander have to bring to bear to accomplish those tasks?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very substantial, physical and mental. And, again, I go back to the -- the idea of prioritisation. And he will wish to ensure that all those things which can be looked after by somebody else are looked after by somebody else. It is -- it is in his interests, therefore, to ensure that he does not have a legacy of either peacetime responsibilities or a legacy of responsibilities that he has -- were created by the ground that he has previously taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, you have reviewed the -- the video of General Cermak -- excuse me, of General Gotovina speaking to his troops on the morning of the 6th. Have you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in that vein, sir, you hear General Gotovina saying some rather -- one might say stern things to his subordinate commanders as he is taking them to the map to move to the next phase of the operation, but he is also turning over the urban regeneration plan, as you call it, to General Cermak in that same meeting. Tell me, General, I mean, as an operational commander, is that something that, if you were in General Gotovina's position, you would welcome and you would look upon as a positive thing for your efforts?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been looking for that support however it might have been presented. I would have been particularly looking for the civil authorities to come and take responsibility for those areas as quickly as they possibly could, to re -- to re-establish normality both within the sort of civil area, including, of course, rule of law. I may have -- I may have shared with General Gotovina, on many occasions, his feelings. I may not quite have expressed it in his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to go into another topic. This might be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Kehoe. We will take a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, if we could talk about a couple of matters that were touched upon by Mr. Cayley. The first one being the active defence order D281.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is the active defence order of the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could go to paragraph 12 in the English. I believe it's the last page. No -- there it is. And if we could put the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just highlight one mistake in the translation here that my colleague Mr. Misetic just noticed. The line that I would like to discuss with the General is in the English, paragraph 12, but if we scroll down in the B/C/S -- page 12 in the B/C/S? Page 12 in the B/C/S. As can you see, it's a paragraph 13 that doesn't exist in the English. We will have that corrected. The comment that I would like to address or the line I would like to address to the General is in the last line of the English paragraph 12, but it is also the last line in the B/C/S paragraph 13. We just noticed that in reviewing it this morning, but we will correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But there are actually two paragraphs 12 in the English. It just is a simple problem. I don't think there is any problem to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In any event, just, General, looking at that last sentence in paragraph 12 in the English, it notes that: "Units shall be timely informed on organised and planned relocation of the Split Military District Knin forward command post from the village of Sajkovici to Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, here, Sajkovici is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea, General, given that this order is the 9th of August, 1995, when the Split Military District forward command post was moved from Sajkovici to Knin and thereafter on to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do refer to it in my report. I can't be absolutely certain. I -- I recall it being between the 15th and 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would -- I would have to be able to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just reference you to page 36 of your report, the -- not the carry-over paragraph but the first full paragraph. I would just like to clarify one issue with you on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put D1084 on the screen, page 36, beginning on line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think it's 1784, if that's the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, 1784, excuse me. Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, looking at that first full paragraph, not the carry-over paragraph but the first full paragraph - and I don't question the substance of your statement that the Croatian authorities were concerned about the effect of looting and burning, and other ill-disciplined acts by the army. But I just want to take you through a sequence of these documents that you put together based on, as we look through, it I'm not going to read the whole thing, the 6th August letter from Colonel Zelic, then followed from -- to a 10 August 1995 letter by senior lieutenant Petar Skoric. And when they talk about these letters, you then follow up with a -- a document which is General Gotovina's order of 20 August 1995. Concerning mop-up operations. And, General, I appreciate that you may not have had the sequence of these documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But if we could bring that document up, and if we could just take a minute and possibly put this in a sequence. It's D102 would be General Gotovina's order. D002 -- excuse me D1002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we, apart from looking at the documents, could I ask you, Mr. Deverell, this paragraph reads: "This was clearly identified on the 6th of August." And then you referred to a letter. And then you say: "This had been preceded on the 10th of August."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is it my error, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was followed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm just asking for D1002 to come up. That's the document that the General cites at footnote 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, General, I appreciate that all these documents might not have been part of the bundle that you had. But as we see in this document, it's an order signed by General Gotovina, an order on operational deployment of HV units and commands. And it notes an order coming from the HV Main Staff, with the appropriate classification numbers. And if we can keep that number in mind and turn to D559. Would you agree with me, General, this is the outgoing order from the Main Staff that is cited by General Gotovina as the basis for setting up these mop-up operations, this order dated 14 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just a nuance to that order, if we will, would be D561 another order from the Main Staff, a day after General Gotovina's order. And in this order, if we look at the -- the second paragraph, again, coming from the Main Staff it notes that: "With a view to organising, planning, searching, and mopping up the ground and the facilities by special units of the MUP intended for these purposes and the military police, as well as with a view to using the HV units for the basic task of fortifying and guarding state orders [sic]." There is then an order - and if we go down to 1.2, if we scroll down the page - essentially orders the HV to go on the borders; and in 1.2, that separate orders will be given to the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could then go to 65 ter 902.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That same day, this is an order from OG West, Operative Group West on 21 August, if you see from the preamble, as MUP forces will be mopping up the remaining Chetnik forces in the field, deep in the area of responsibility of OG West with the aim of ensuring safety ... then gives orders to his individual commanders or individual units subordinate to Colonel Fuzul, the Operative Group West commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, if we could offer 65 ter 902 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no objection on principle, but Mr. Kehoe went through three, four, five documents extremely quickly. The Registrar could barely keep up on the screen. And now the document's being offered without any questions. I'm not objecting to its admissibility; I'm just wondering what we're doing exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm not going to invite you to explain in full detail what you are doing. I noticed that, but perhaps I should also address Mr. Hedaraly, but all questions put in relation to the last three or four documents we saw on our screen there seems not to be much dispute about one order with the same number following another one that there is a link. And then we now got a new document, that's the first time we see this one, without any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, but I'm going to go into a question right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm not -- is there anything which you consider to be in dispute which you would like to -- to raise in relation to this document? Because I would be hesitant to add another document hearing evidence on matters as, for the last three or four document, not in dispute. But if there's anything in dispute, if you'd like to -- or seek something that we don't know already from Mr. Deverell, then we'd like to here those questions. Mr. Registrar, the number of this document would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last document on this series is the -- two days later from General Markac, P2376.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is a document, General, that General Markac of the Ministry of the Interior discusses the actual mop-up operations. So going back to the -- putting your citation to the order of General Gotovina in context, it would appear that that citation is a bit out of context, because General Gotovina and Split Military District forces aren't involved in mop-up operations, number one; and number two, this particular citation doesn't necessarily follow from the other two. Appreciating, General, that you didn't have all these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very happy to accept that. My point of listing all those documents was to demonstrate that there was a great deal of activity going on during that period, in terms of planning, planning not only for ongoing operations but also for the normalisation of the area that had been - if I may use the term "liberated" - and General Cermak did not seem part of either the information or action -- there was no requirement for his action because he was sent -- he was not sent the majority of those documents, if any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Moving back to your report, and I would like to talk a little bit about the subordination issues that you outline both de jure and de facto. And I think in page 35 of your report at line 14 and 15, you note that taking the job as a garrison commander was simply a means to an end. Do you recall that, sir? And that's again on line 14 through 16 of page 35 of your report, D1784.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this was not a -- with regard to General Cermak with his unique tasks; it was not a unique garrison commander situation. And, in fact, you note that Major Gojevic was the actual garrison commander doing the normal garrison commander items, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my deduction from what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now taking that -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you said "it was not a unique garrison ... situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should have been -- it was -- it was a unique -- it should be "it was a unique garrison position" to the extent I put a "not" in there, I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on page 40 -- or, excuse me, 39 of your report, and I'm referring to lines 17 through 23, and also on page 42, lines 18 through 19, you note that there is an lack of communication between General Gotovina and General Cermak, but, likewise, a lack of communication between General Cermak and General Gotovina. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you use the term in page 42 at page 18 -- excuse me, line 18 -- that General Cermak is largely fell out of the loop, that largely falling out of the loop goes both ways, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when we look at -- at -- putting aside the situation where -- where General Cermak asked General Gotovina's help in finding the vehicles with the subordinate brigades, I mean, you don't find any letters -- let me back that up. I think we talked about the ORBAT that you had as well as other orders, combat orders by General Gotovina not being sent to the Knin garrison, but we also have, throughout your report, documentation between, for instance, UN entities or ICRC discussing crime, looting, burning, murder, those types of documents. While you see General Cermak giving those other documents concerning crime to other people. You don't see any documents concerning looting, burning, and murder that come to the attention of General Cermak being sent to General Gotovina, do you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in that vein, it would -- in the scheme of what was happening in Knin after Operation Storm, you would agree with me that, based on the record, General Cermak wasn't turning to General Gotovina as a person to fight criminal activity. Putting aside the UN vehicle situation, but everything else.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree. There was none of the normal passage of information, the routine passage of information that I would have expected to see between one headquarters and another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the other matters that you talked about and -- General Cermak being sent down there and having that position as a means to an end, I mean, one of the themes that -- that runs through your report and the documentation as well as much evidence in this -- in this case - I cite the statement of Mr. Radin at D1678, that General Cermak is being sent down there to normalise life. I'm sure you've seen that on numerous occasions. Now, on that score, you don't see any reports going from General Cermak to General Gotovina or General Gotovina to General Cermak on this normalisation of life issue, do you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, I think you also note in your report that, either by design or by happenstance, General Cermak became the point of contact for the international organisations. Now, likewise, you don't see any reporting from General Cermak to General Gotovina on the issue of contact with international organisations, do you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not apart from those issues you have already identified, the UNCRO vehicles and -- and the like, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there is certainly no orders going from General Gotovina to General Cermak saying, Do X, Y, and Z with regard to international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I take it that is also true there are no orders coming from General Gotovina with regard to normalisation life of issues directed to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There appears to be little interest in this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on -- on the -- what you cited in your report, that you believe it was justified for General Gotovina to let General Cermak get on with his business, while he, General Gotovina, as an operational commander got on with his.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure the word "justified" was necessarily used. I can understand it. As I have said before, I think I would have done the same thing. I would have been very happy that there was somebody else who had a -- a particular rank who could answer some of the problems, particularly opposed by the international community, that might distract me from what I felt quite properly was my primary objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be accurate to say that both gentlemen, General Gotovina, in his area of responsibility, and General Cermak, in his area of responsibility, were doing essential their own things and conducting what they thought they needed to do, basically leaving each other alone.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the situation that turned -- that was the situation which it turned into, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, one last thing, and, General I do this by clarification, if I may, and I address the issue of -- of the confusion concerning General Cermak's role. I believe, that we -- you had the -- definition of military governor put on the screen with Mr. Cayley. And in your statement, you talk a bit, if I may, page 50, going over to the top of page 51, that General Gotovina may have added to the confusion concerning the responsibilities or the title of General Cermak. And you cite the meeting of the 8th of August, 1995, and that would be P359. And that's cited at your report at page 51, footnote 201. And this is a recounting meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just bring it up on the screen quickly. If we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, in the first paragraph, the commander's assessment at 1A, we talk about the meeting both with General Cermak and there was also a meeting with General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the English, 3A1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is just basically when General Gotovina directs General Forand to General Cermak for any efforts. And you -- it says for lines down: "He," being General Gotovina, "noted that commander Sector South had already met with Colonel General Cermak, military governor, and stated that all problems should be able to be resolve with the military governor who will remain in Knin until the civil authority can be established." And, General, I just want to address with you just for one moment the source of that confusion, because we -- we have this terminology being used on the 8th. And I want to refer you back to the first meeting with -- with General Cermak and -- and General Forand that took place on the 7th. And that would be P356. And, General, this is -- the record is clear, this is before General Forand even met with General Gotovina. And at P356, General, is a sitrep that's dated 8 August 1995 at 0730 hours. But it recounts a meeting that took place on 7th of August.
