utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could go do the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, General Forand is talking about a meeting with General Cermak where it notes at paragraph 8 at the bottom: "Report of meeting, commander Sector South, military governor region. Commander Sector South met with General Cermak in the military governor headquarters." Now, without going into the substance of this, it appears that even prior to -- or prior to any meeting with General Gotovina, General Forand has some -- has latched on to this ill-grounded description of the military governor. So it's Forand who carries it on and not General Gotovina, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I read, it appeared to me that General Gotovina had used that phrase. If further study of the documents demonstrates that that phrase was in common use beforehand, certainly by Brigadier-General Forand, I'm very prepared to review it. It doesn't change my essential point that this whole thing was an unwitting misunderstanding which I believe probably General Forand was responsible for, for reasons that I touched on before, and not a deliberate attempt to mislead by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, isn't it true that on page 51 of your report you already explained this. To say, Well, it was perhaps mistranslated or misinterpreted, but whatever the reason was, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that is my -- that's my belief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was quite clear from your report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kuzmanovic, you are the one who will cross-examine Mr. Deverell?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac, and he will now cross-examined you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to follow up on the first theme that Mr. Kehoe discussed relating to two exhibits. The first exhibit being D409.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If that could be pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: D409 was a 2nd of August meeting in the Republic of Croatia Defence Ministry. Part of that meeting dealt with operational concerns in which both General Gotovina and General Markac were present. As you stated, General, the minutes note that General Cermak was not present. On page 5 of that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe had discussed with you through this document and you had discussed it yourself, General, that at 1730, in the minister's office, there was meeting discussing basically post-conflict security issues. And neither General Gotovina nor General Cermak nor General Markac are in on this particular meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that if General Markac was responsible for any post-conflict security, he would have been present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't necessarily draw that conclusion, because I hadn't looked at it from that point of view. The fact that he was not there clearly indicates that he was not party to the discussion. What role he might have played, subsequently, I think is a matter for further investigation with the police. To me, it's a mark of lack of preparation. But he was not there. Therefore, he could not have been party to those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's fair to state, General, that nothing in terms of what anything that you have read could lead you to the conclusion that General Markac had any role in post-conflict security after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing I've read directs me to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Similarly, if we look at D45. If we look at D45, this is an August 4th 1995 meeting, a working meeting between the Ministry of Interior and, basically, the Ministry of Police Administration, Military Police Administration. Again, preparation during the post-offensive operations is discussed. Is this a document that you had seen before, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at the first page, there's a list of people there from the Ministry of Interior, including Mr. Moric, who was at the previous meeting.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. If we go to the next page, General Lausic is there from the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Among others. There is no General Cermak, General Markac, or General Gotovina present at this particular meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, could I seek some clarification. In one of your previous questions referring to the 1730, the half past 5.00 in the afternoon meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said this was about post-conflict security. I see there are two matters specifically dealt with in this meeting, the one is the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other one is refugees. Now, I'm inclined to agree with you that these are post-conflict matters. But I would like to -- post-conflict security matters. Mr. Deverell, you said that Mr. Markac did not -- well, was not involved in post-conflict security. First of all, when did you consider the conflict to have ended, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is a very difficult question, and I really am not sure I could give a definitive answer, Your Honour. There was much confusion as there always will in this, for example, the civil authority -- one sign the civil authority was re-establishing Knin was by the opening of the police station on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be -- let me try to make the question more simple for you. At the 10th of August, was the conflict -- had the conflict ended, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the initial operational part of the conflict had ended. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It means that if we are talking about post-conflict, that we have to know what you mean by that. And that might not necessarily be exactly the same as what Mr. Kuzmanovic has on his mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... This -- Mr. Kuzmanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to be as clear as possible. Second, do you, apart from the two items mentioned in this half past 5.00 meeting, would you consider mop-up operations later on in August post-conflict security matters, or would you say, No, that's not what I refer to in my answer when I said that Mr. Markac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would consider those to be part of the post-conflict phase because it is part of the reestablishment of law and order and the reestablishment of the rule of law, rather than what I might describe as the conventional operational stage against -- phase against formed bodies of -- of troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in my question, I addressed the issue of post-conflict or not, and another matter was security. Did you consider mopping-up operations to be part of this post-conflict security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I would do. I have to say that I was -- was not asked to look at the civil police issue, and -- and the associated parts of the civil police. So I only -- I only looked at it in terms of how it impinged upon General Cermak. And, therefore, I think it is a very difficult area. But I would see operations as part of - those operations, mop-up operations - as part of the post-conflict phase. Now when it started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I have difficulty being clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was part -- it was a security matter as well, you said earlier. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is it true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I take you back to your answer and to the question put to you by Mr. Kuzmanovic. He asked you: "It fair to say, General, that nothing in terms of what anything that you have read could lead you to the conclusion that General Markac had any role in post-conflict security after Operation Storm?" And you said: "Nothing I have read directs me to that, no." That would then include, in view of the answers to my previous questions, that it is your testimony - and it's just for a matter of clarity that I'm asking you these questions - that you would say that nothing could lead you to the conclusion that General Markac had any role in mop-up operations after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- be included in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I go back, Your Honour, please, because I need to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was addressing the precise question that I was posed from the point of view of that meeting which dealt with only refugees and check-points and the absence of General Markac, because it was clear that he had no role to play in that. I think I would have to say that mop-up operations, in my judgement, would be part of the post-conflict operations. And, therefore, General Markac would have had an interest in those because he was commanding a capability which -- which -- had a role to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm seeking this clarification because words are pronounced very quickly and it is of great importance that both the one who puts the question and the one who answers the question is fully aware of what the language means. And just briefly making an observation in relation to the last part of your answer, the question was that "nothing in terms of what anything that you have read could lead you to the conclusion that ..." which is a very broad approach. And I now do understand that you focussed primarily on what you read in relation to this meeting that was brought to your attention just the minutes before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could pull up D1788 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is -- Mr. Kehoe mentioned this document earlier, and this is specifically related to mop-up operations. This is the 21st of August, 1995, order from the Main Staff of the Croatian army, requesting that and ordering the Special Police forces to mop-up the remaining forces. It says Chetnik forces in the field. Now, from the standpoint of military operations, this is an order from the military to the Special Police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a look at who signed it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of OG West.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to D561, 121788 [sic] is the order directed to the Special Police, but D561 is the Main Staff order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that there are elements it notes in this order of enemy renegade groups remaining in the liberated areas and with a view to organising, planning, searching, and mopping up the ground. I'll slow down. And the facilities by special units of the Ministry of Interior. And it's signed by the chief of the Main Staff on the second page, General Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now this is an order essentially from the Main Staff to the Special Police, among others, for conduct of mop-up operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in your estimation, this is a military issue, not a civilian police issue; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that it's been signed by the Chief of Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to your report, General, page 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think this issue has come up before with this particular document. I had thought it had been resolved. The translation of the -- of the recipients says Knin ZP in the translation. We've looked at this before; it is ZM, it is the Knin garrison. I think that has been discussed at length before, and I thought a revised translation was being done. I don't know what happened, but just so that the witness is aware of that. If -- I don't know if that has anything to do with the question but just in case. So that -- just for the benefit of the witness that he has the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the original, at least, states ZM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think for purposes of my question -- I understand that. I will go to 2376, because I think it will make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to P2376, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the issue concerning the previous document, General, you can see with this document on the 22nd August, 1995, the mop-up operation report, from General Markac, goes directly to the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I see the signature just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sure I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 3.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 3. Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at least as far as the mop-up operations are concerned, those are essentially being controlled, at least according to the documents, from the Main Staff to the special units of the Special Police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would appear so, yes. I don't think I've ever seen that document. I don't recognise it. I don't think this is in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess we can go back to page 52 of the report, lines 12 to 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, in this section of your report, you're discussing a freedom of movement generally, and you cite a document which is P359, for General Forand's comment, that the Special Police were supplanting the HV, basically the working military, and being abrasive, arrogant, and dismissive. Now, other than -- what was the purpose for citing this particular document, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of a -- a group of documents that I looked at in terms of the freedom of movement and whether freedom of movement was effectively allocated to UNCRO and who was responsible for it and whether they had met that responsibility. It was really to give a flavour of the atmosphere to give some sort of context to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as the representation made in this particular exhibit, whether it was the military police or the Special Police that were identified at that particular time, you have no information, do you, whether that is accurate?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the comment from the Sector South report as my primary source. I did not check as to whether that comment itself was accurate. As I say, it was a matter of giving a context, rather than the actual fact that I felt was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the -- sorry, if I can just finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It showed the way General Forand's mind was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The specific date of this report, P ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- 359 is the 8th of August of 1995, I'll represent that to you without pulling it up.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Special Police were essentially through with their axis of operation by the 8th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically. I didn't look for that sort of information either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information that the Special Police were ever in Knin at any time?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go do -- the second portion of your report on page 52, lines 22 through 27.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, page 52, I'm sorry. The same page.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20 -- I'm sorry. I'm confused now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Lines 22 through 27.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, again, there is a citation for your report, P362, in which General Forand again states that various malfeasance was being conducted by agencies of the Croatian government, usually behind the restriction of movement enforced by Croatian Special Police. Now, again the purpose of citing that document was just for contextual reasons?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And whether or not the Croatian Special Police were the ones involved as Forand asserts, you have no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge. And, again, I was trying to show how General Forand was thinking about this issue and his response to these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What about -- is there anything about that -- you have twice now mentioned General Forand's thinking and his reactions. Is there anything about that that you're critical of?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I mean, he -- he only thought what -- I mean, he based his -- I will start that again. He would have based his thoughts, his ideas, on what he was being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And whether that was accurate or not was a function of the information he was getting?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And, of course, part of his responsibility would have been to judge how accurate that information was. But, my experience in these areas is that is it extraordinarily difficult to know what is true. You know what have you been told, but to know what is true is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at least from the documents that you have seen, was there any follow-up by General Forand to determine whether the information he was receiving was accurate?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure he did. But I have seen no documents where he checked the accuracy of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Hedaraly to cross-examine the witness, could I take you back to D561. Could that be brought on the screen. You were asked, Mr. Deverell, and I repeat literally what Mr. Kuzmanovic said: "Now, this is an order essentially from the Main Staff to the Special Police, among others, for conduct of mop-up operations; correct?" And you said: "Yes." Could you perhaps elaborate on -- Mr. Kuzmanovic, I was correct in understanding that your question was about D561?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you tell me exactly where we find the Special Police to be addressed in this order and given orders for the conduct of mop-up operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I took my view, if I read the document correctly, that that paragraph, with a view to organising, planning, searching, and mopping up the ground in the facilities by special units of the Ministry of Interior intended for the purposes, et cetera, et cetera, as well as using the HV units for the basic task of -- of guarding the state borders, I hereby issue the following order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the context is mop-up operations to be conducted with the assistance of others by MUP units. I see that context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was not whether this was an order which related to MUP operations. The question was whether this order, essentially, was from the Main Staff to the Special Police, orders for conduct of mop-up operations. Which I understand to be, is that the Main Staff would have ordered the MUP to conduct mop-up operations. And, therefore, I looked at -- also at what is then exactly ordered. And I would invite you to do the same and then to point at where orders are given to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I -- could I just ask for it be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can look at it page by page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, 1.2 says that, of course, separate orders shall be issued. And this was, of course, also requiring which resulted in some other correspondence. This was asking - if can I scroll up slightly, please - it says the commanders -- the commanders of Knin garrison shall prepare reports and submit them to the General Staff in a descriptive form et cetera, giving details of areas of contact with remaining or infiltrated enemy groups, and so on and so forth. And it then goes on, at one point, to -- that separate orders shall be issued. If I could use a military term, if the Court will allow me, this would, to me, be a warning order for a future operation. That is, it begins the process of analysis and deciding and planning that would lead to a future operation. So from my point of view, the order is that this work is to start. It is not a specific order. And therefore, Your Honour, I would agree, I think, with the question you're trying to ask me, It is not a specific order to the Special Police to conduct an operation. This is a warning order which generates the work before that order is -- is -- is written and issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, often the attention of this Chamber was drawn to the way in which the addressees were mentioned. If we look at the very end of this order - in English - I think it was you who told us that for information means a kind of a courtesy rather than -- could you perhaps look at to whom this order is sent or to whom it is addressed, because the top say to the commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is addressed, in particular, to - and there, Knin ZP, I believe, should be Knin ZM, and I think that was the nature of the previous intervention from the Prosecution - and right at the bottom, handwritten, the assistant MUP for special units for information only. Now that, in a sense, is part and parcel of the warning order process. It -- it wouldn't have been in the British Army, it would have been an action addressee, because the warning order is an order. But the information of this order was passed to the headquarters, the MUP headquarters, for passage to the special units. That is the way I would interpret that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you these questions because there was quick question taking three lines, the answer was even shorter, just a yes, whereas, now going through this document, it seems that the matter has more details and the matter has more aspects than were dealt with in your answer. Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Deverell? Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Deverell, and he is about to start his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just before I start, while we have this document on the screen, perhaps we don't have it anymore. Just very quickly, that was an order from General Cervenko to, among others, General Cermak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it asked him to report -- to perform a certain task; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I first want to ask you briefly a few questions regarding the additional note that you prepared.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which is D1786.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Actually, perhaps at the outset, Mr. President, I should state that I have reviewed the revised report which is D1784, which we MFI'd. There are no objections. The only think I would note is that the corrigendum, D1758, which are the changes in the report, the pages listed in the additional note do not match. There is a three-page difference. So if it says page 10 in the addendum, it's page 13. I have discussed the issue with Mr. Cayley last week. I'm wondering, for the sake of the record, although I put that on the record today, I think it may be wiser to have a revised corrigendum so that for the future anyone looking at the report will note precisely which changes were made in which page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the corrigendum, let me see, was not a document which was signed by the witness, was it? It's mainly -- if it was, then, of course, it is a difficult to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, in fact -- sorry, Mr. Hedaraly -- maybe was not updated about this, and that may be my fault. But, in fact, the corrigendum has been updated so it matches the report. Because what Mr. Hedaraly kindly pointed out before is that the numbering sequence in the updated report didn't match the old report. So what the witness did was to change it to the old report. If you understand what I mean, so, in essence, the corrigendum and the report now match each other in terms of numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sure that's a matter I can resolve with Mr. Cayley at the break, Your Honour, there's no need to spend time on it this second. And we will report back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the Chamber received information of which the original was: "This is to let you know that the corrigendum, 2D00791, additional note, 2D00729, and corrected version of Sir Jack Deverell's report, 2D00790, are all available on e-court. The previous versions of the corrigendum and report page numbers did not match up." And then that was a message which was sent --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I did receive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that seems to be the answer to the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's not actually, Mr. President, and that's why I -- perhaps I was not clear in my intervention earlier. Maybe if we just look at D1758 now in the record we will see that that -- the page numbers listed in that corrigendum do not match the pages in the report that I was looking at. As I said, I'm more than happy to discuss the matter with Mr. Cayley and resolve it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please discuss with Mr. Cayley whether consolidated versions of all these documents are now available in e-court so as to avoid that those who will read it later are puzzled by it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry, General, for the little interruption. I wanted to discuss with you the additional note you prepared briefly at the outset. That is D1786. We can bring it on the screen, if necessary. You first state that you were contacted by the Cermak Defence team on 27 January 2008. Now, prior to that date, did you know either General Markac -- General Cermak or anyone on General Cermak's team?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know how you came to be selected or contacted to be an expert in this case?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. In fact, I apparently had met Mr. Cayley who remembered me when he was in the British army. So, yes, there had been some contact. Sadly, I don't think I quite remembered him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I try to forget him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we give a few words of confidence to Mr. Cayley in a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Not that I'm a witness, I was a very junior officer at the time, Mr. President. And General Deverell was a General at the time. So I wasn't exactly on friendly terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- and Mr. Kehoe will apologise after this court session for his words. Mr. Cayley, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've distracted myself now. I forgot what your question was. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I had asked you whether you knew how you came to --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think you answered it that Mr. Cayley contacted you because he knew you from before.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may have been so. But, in fact, I also met a senior British officer who been previously involved in various International Criminal Court and ICTY cases, and he asked me, because he knew there was some coming that required expert witness, and he asked me if I was interested. And I said yes. And, in fact, I believe my name was passed to whoever by what means and then the connection was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to this case, have you testified before as an expert?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And once you were formally retained as an expert by the Cermak Defence, what were your precis terms of reference?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent some terms of reference. I can't recall them. I mean, I'm not quite sure what question you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What were you asked to do as an expert?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked do look at the case with particular attention to quite clearly Mr. Cermak, General Cermak, and concentrate really on the command and control issues, and relate all that to the -- the military and also the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you hired to -- were you retained to prepare an expert report, to consult with the Cermak Defence, or both?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I was retained to produce -- to produce an expert report. I'm not quite sure what you mean by "consult." There was quite clearly a very important link between me and the Defence team, because they -- they understood the background to the case, and, of course, they had the documents which they fed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps my -- my question was not clear. And if that is the case, I apologise. I was asking whether, as part of your tasks, one of them was to provide advice or expertise to the Cermak Defence team, separate from preparing the expert report. So whether they would ask you questions and you would advise them generally on various issues of command and control.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I have done, as well as write the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And at that initial meeting with the Cermak Defence team, were you told what was the position of -- of the Cermak Defence with respect to General Cermak's authority, as they viewed it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure of the -- I don't really understand the question. Can you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course. When you were -- when you met with the Cermak Defence team and they told you that they were interested in this case and General Cermak and the issues of his authority, did they tell you what their position was with respect to these issues?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was -- at all stages, I said in my additional note, at everyone stage I was -- right the start it was made absolutely clear that it was my -- my business to make judgements from the documents I was given and -- and quite obviously from the conversations that were had because that is the nature of the -- the dynamic of being part of -- you know, working for that team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, could I seek clarification. The one doesn't exclude the other, and, therefore, even if someone tells you that you should form your opinion on the basis of the documents you have received, that doesn't exclude for the possibility that someone, at the same time, tells you what his view on certain matters are. So, therefore, I'm a bit puzzled by your answer. Could you be clearer in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps my answer was confusing because I am particularly keen to emphasise that I was given a complete, as it were, blank sheet. I discussed matters. Of course, I heard their views, because that is an inevitable way you discuss matter. But, whenever there was a view issued or at a particular time, I have to emphasise that I was instructed that it had to be my judgement and my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your previous answer, you said: "And quite obviously from the conversations that were had because that is the nature of the -- the dynamic of being part of -- you know, working for that team." So I do understand that you wanted to end that sentence by saying that you became familiar with their views.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, I have matched up the dates of your present in The Hague when you said you came and listened to court proceedings with the witnesses that testified, and I just want to confirm that those are the testimonies that you attended in person. That was General Leslie?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not here -- I did not see Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You did not see his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you see any other testimonies of any other witnesses in The Hague while you were also in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no. I think those are the only three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you watch the testimony of any other witnesses, either over the Internet, through a DVD that may have been provided, or any other manner?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- yes I did. I switched on the -- I went on to the Internet every so often. To be honest, I can't remember whose testimony I saw, because I was -- I was looking at it out of general interest rather than specific interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So nothing you would have seen in those proceedings were a significant --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- portion --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- that you relied on for your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you review transcripts of testimony of any witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you tell us which ones, please.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely specific. But I was given the transcripts of witnesses such as Flynn, Elleby, Botteri, Feldi, Leslie and, of course, I had Theunens's report and listened to much of that cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were these transcripts of testimony provided to you because you asked for them, or were you given to you as material you should review?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given to me as material that I should review.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you review any witness statements from any of the witnesses -- any of the witness statements in this case?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I see some, but I frankly can't recall the ones that I did see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if you had seen those statements, once again, that's not something that you have relied in any significant manner for your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it's been the background to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You mentioned some names. Let me just mention a few others. I won't go through all the witnesses for obvious reasons, but just a few ones to see if it jogs your memory. Did you view the statement or transcript testimony of General Forand?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was sent Lausic. I'd have to check, actually, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But the fact that you don't remember, it means you didn't pay particular attention to it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Eric Hendriks?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Stjepan Buhin?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Bosko Dzolic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. The trouble is, I -- I read so much that was produced by him that I have difficulty remembering exactly where I saw it. Mostly they were the documents. But I don't think I saw a transcript from Dzolic, but I might have done -- and I could check. If it is important for the Court, I could go back to my records and check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we leave that for Mr. Hedaraly. If he --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he thinks that we should be informed about it, then he'll invite you to check or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or he will refrain from doing so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I do appreciate the offer. I mean, all I'm trying to assess is what you relied on and how much significance you gave to it. So if you had reviewed the evidence of Mr. Dzolic, you did not rely on it in any significant manner for your report. So is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did consult with Mr. Feldi or Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consulted on a couple of technical details with General Feldi, yes, in terms of, right at the beginning, to get a view of -- of the nature of the -- of the Croatian army and armed forces and how they did their business, particularly in terms of -- of training and promotion -- selection for promotion and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is that the meeting you had with him or was it a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I met him face-to-face in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: How many meetings did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, a couple. I don't know -- they were not formal meetings so much as he was in the office, and I remember speaking to him on one occasion for perhaps an hour, and then I might pop in to his office or he might come into mine and I might have a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What about Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall ever talking to him about anything in particular. But I might have -- again, I might have, in passing, I might have asked him a question. But it would not have been a substantial one. It would have been about background.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you did not discuss with either Mr. Feldi or Mr. Kovacevic the substance of what you have put in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't think I ever discussed with them the -- my -- my views, my -- the observations I -- I ended up, my judgements, no. It was -- it was a matter of discussing, putting in context some of the information that I had so that I was given confidence I was making the right judgement or a reasonable judgement, not so much the right one, but a reasonable judgement from that which I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: A reasonable judgement as to what?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reasonable judgement as to whether I had drawn the right conclusions from my reading of something against what the Croatian armed forces actually did. Again, it was mostly about command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if you looked at a certain document, an order, or a report, and you drew some conclusions from that, you, at times, sought Mr. Feldi's assistance to confirm that your interpretation was correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That I -- that I had understood the facts and drawn the correct conclusions. But, again, it was specifically about things like command and control, about structures, about the nature of -- of how the Croatian Army did its business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you review Mr. Feldi's expert report or any draft thereof?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at most of Mr. Feldi's expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you provide any comments to either Mr. Feldi or the Cermak Defence team with respect to that report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you review the expert report of Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you consult with Mr. Albiston on any issues?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were together, we talked about the case. We had mutual interest because both our experiences were very similar in our lives, particularly focussed on Northern Ireland. And where there was a cross over between police operations and military operations, undoubtedly I discussed things with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how many discussions had you had with him on these issues?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't possibly say. We were together for four or five days in Zagreb at one stage, and we were together here on occasions, listening to various testimonies. And rather like my conversations with Mr. Feldi, it was not a formal meeting where we sat down with an agenda; it was discussions in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But you discussed with him the substance of the case; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you exchange views and opinions with respect to the issues that you addressed in your report and that he addressed in his?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure we did. Again, if you're together and have a mutual interest, you would wish to express that interest to see if the judgements you were coming to were -- were supportable, were they understandable, how had you expressed it? I mean, very often we were looking at, How do we express this? This is very complex issues; there are some very complex issues here. How do we get people to understand the nature of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of two of these very complex issues that you discussed and grappled with together?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command and control of the military police. The reality of it, not what is written down, the reality of that complexity. And that is very important. Because what happens on the ground is sometimes rather different under the pressure of events than what is written down in the paper. And that is something we have both experienced in our police and military careers and, I mean, that is one example I know of a conversation we did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So the section in your --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. It's my fault, Your Honour. I'm talking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, it's usually my fault. I get scolded repeatedly by the transcribers, the interpreters, and the Presiding Judge. If I can seek your assistance in pausing, that will hopefully help me not to get scolded as much. Just to go back to your previous answer, so, for example, the issue of command and control of the military police, which you have addressed in your report, would, in part, be informed by conversations you had with Mr. Albiston. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that is correct. I think you're trying to draw a different conclusion from -- from my words. Everything you do is in informed by -- by the conversations you have around you, by things you hear. If you're saying - and you may not be saying - but I included quite consciously some of Mr. Albiston's thoughts, that is not true. If you're saying that all my report is the -- is the focus of all of conversations I had with a wide -- with a very substantial number of people, then, of course, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just so you know, I was not inferring any impropriety. I was referring to the latter of the examples, just so that you know. You also state in your report that you were sent over 4.000 separate documents by the Cermak Defence team. Did you review them all?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly didn't. And the figure 4.000 was -- was a -- something of a throw-away line. There were many hundreds of them, and I guess it was into the thousands, some of which, of course, as yet not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, before we start with the 4.000 or the couple of hundred, perhaps it's -- would this be an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think it probably would be, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because, you know, if you have one or two questions to finish a certain subject, I will let you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have a suspicion, based on the last answer, that it may be a little more lengthy than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, we will first take the break. We will have a break and resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, before the break, we were discussing the documents that you had received and reviewed, and I asked you about the 4.000 figure and you stated that that figure was probably just a general, a throw-away line, and not the accurate number of documents and that you have probably reviewed several hundreds and went into the thousands. Is that an accurate --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify the timing of these documents. So you were initially provided with a collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many that collection comprised?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't, I'm afraid. I mean, I got the documents, Your Honour, over a period of time, and, indeed, up until -- some up until just before I received -- I wrote the report. And I would suggest it was a steady flow of documents. The first package was quite large, probably a thousand or some sort, but I have no clear -- I can't give you any clear identification of exactly how they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you received -- would it be fair to say that you had not completed the review of the initial documents you received when you received new ones. It was a rolling basis?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So it wasn't a sequential review of the number of documents, then you got more documents, and then so on; it was a steady production of documents?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A steady, flow, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in your additional note you state that on 12 and 13 March of this year, Mr. Cayley identified and grouped documents for you relevant to each heading of your report. Were these documents additional documents, or were they subsets of documents that had you already been provided?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority were subsets of documents I'd already been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you estimate, if possible for us, the size of the collection of documents you were provided by categories, but headings?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think -- I think that which Mr. Cayley gave me were -- were hundreds of documents rather than thousands, which were related -- specific ones which were related to the subject headings that he wished me to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would I be correct in stating that a number of these documents you had already reviewed?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And a number of documents were new to you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were new. But the majority, I think, I had reviewed. I think I can -- yes, I think the majority I had reviewed. There might have been the odd one or two, a dozen or so, that were perhaps new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were these documents, the ones that Mr. Cayley provided to you in separate groupings for each of the headings, were they primarily the documents that you referenced in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, there are other ones I reference in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But the majority of them are in that --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, ask the Cermak Defence team for any specific documentation that you felt was lacking?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically asking them. In our conversations, documents would be discussed and I would say, Well, can you please send me that one. If you ask me which one I talked about, I can't give it to you, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you review the interviews General Cermak provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I had -- I had access to them, and I remember reading parts of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But that's not something that you relied on significantly in the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't quote it in my report. It was, again, background information as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was going to come to that, but perhaps we can address it now while we're at the topic. The documents that you have not referenced in your report, did you consider them to be background material?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. And also partly I felt, on occasions, that I had sufficient -- let me use the word "evidence" in a loose sense. I had sufficient information to make the point I was trying to make. I could support my -- my view in a way which I felt would allow people to see that it was a reasonable view to take, given the evidence that I had produced. There were certainly have been more evidence or more information that I would have been looking at but decided not reference it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what was the process by which you specifically selected -- I haven't counted them but roughly 100 or so documents in your report from the hundreds and maybe thousands of documents that you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it goes back to my -- my methodology. I was particularly keen to, first of all, understand the nature of the problem that I was -- that I had been asked to deal with. I then read what I thought would be the key documents to give me that understanding. And when I had got to that stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt the witness, but the transcript has actually stopped recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The one on the main screen is functioning, so perhaps we can refer to that while the problem gets fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could we continue to work on that basis and see whether ... Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If there is a need to refer to earlier testimony, we'll see how we can do it. But for now, I think we will be fine for the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You said in your last answer -- just trying to find it exactly. You said: "I then read what I thought would be the key documents to give me that understanding." How did you -- was that your determination that these were key documents, or were they part of the ones provided to you and said, These are the key documents?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my determination as to what were the key documents, and they were essentially -- because I wished to focus initially on what the exact -- what was Croatian military doctrine, military law, Code of Discipline, laws of the regulations of service, and so on and so forth, to give me a background in -- in understanding the nature of the force and the way it was structured. I then wanted to see what responsibilities and authorities a garrison commander and therefore General Cermak might have had. And then I looked for evidence as to whether he actually had that authority and how he had exercised it. So there was a sort of process of understanding the nature of -- of the Croatian armed forces, the specific nature of General Cermak's responsibilities, and then how did he manage those responsibilities, in the rather confused situation he found himself and in the unusual situation he found himself, as we will no doubt discuss, as a Colonel General, as a garrison commander, doing other things as well. And so, therefore, I looked at the documents from this point of view. I went in to find out the answers to those particular questions. As best I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the documents that you referenced in the footnotes in your report are the key documents that you relied on to reach your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so -- I think that would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And these would be the documents that you feel are the most important and that the Chamber should rely on as well in making its determination, regarding General Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I can't speak for the Chamber, but I can only say that, as far as I am concerned, they were the key documents that enabled me to come to the judgements I came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was there anything in the other documents that you reviewed that are not referenced in your report that contradicted your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I -- I think if they had done, then I may have altered my conclusions. And -- and if there are documents which are produced which I didn't see or misinterpreted that have an impact upon my conclusions then, of course, I'm happy to review my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You also stated in your report that you were able to talk to General Cermak. How often did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once, and, really, that was a very informal contact. And it was, really, talking in generalities. I did not pose him any particular questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just so that I am clear, you did not ask any specific questions to General Cermak regarding information you were looking for to prepare your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I asked him one question: Why have they decided to make a garrison commander a Colonel-General? And he answered it. And that was the way Croatia did its -- did that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In terms of your report, we talked briefly about the headings. You said you were given a series of headings to address and that you were invited to add any headings that you thought were relevant. Did you, in fact, add any such headings other that the ones provided to by Mr. Cayley, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because I felt that those headings covered the essential nature of what I was generally asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The last meeting in your additional note that you described with the Cermak Defence team is dated 19 and 20 October that you met with Mr. Cayley. Did you meet with anyone from the Cermak Defence team between the 20th of October and the time you began your testimony here on Friday?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met with Mr. Cayley and briefly Mr. Kay in -- in The Hague here, in the -- in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you meet with members of the Defence team of General Gotovina or General Markac?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, prior to Friday.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met both Mr. Kehoe and - I'm terribly sorry I'm going destroy your name - Mr. Kuzmanovic. It's not, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's Kuzmanovic. We all know who he is.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Him over there. I'm very sorry about that. I apologise. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the purpose of these meetings were simply to go through the questions that you were going to be posed?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was really to identify some of the issues that my report -- they saw in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm simply asking because the additional note only covered the period until 20th October.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which is fine.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And while you were in The Hague last week, did you meet with Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We were staying in the same hotel. I -- but he was, at that stage, giving evidence and therefore avoided me. Quite properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Before he gave evidence, did you meet with him in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He arrived late one night, and I -- I believe went straight in to give evidence the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, sorry to interrupt you. The server has been restarted. If you open the transcript again and then push the "connect" button, then the whole of the transcript is available to the parties again. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour, as I'm sure my colleagues are as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you need any attention, please -- I see you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I seem to be stuck, but that's not unusual in my case with these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you open the 9th of November, open the folder, then you select transcript, then you get the transcript, but in order to make it moving, you should connect at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm being ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If there's any urgent need to stop, we can do so obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for those background questions. The next topic I'd like to discuss with you briefly is just general principles of command and control which you discussed in your report. And I just want you to bear in mind this first series of questions is really general in nature, so I'm not asking anything about General Cermak or General Gotovina but just wanting to look at some of your statements and ask you for further information.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we start at page 10 of your report. You probably don't even need to refer to these, because they're probably quite well known to you. But you state: "Both these commissions documents require officers to respond to breaches of military discipline which by some means are brought to their attention, whether committed by soldiers under their command or not. The form of response will vary." I just want to stop here for a second, and we will go to the next sentence for my next question so that I'm clear on that sentence. If a commander - and I'm talking generally here - if a commander learns about a breach of a military by a soldier, he must - and I understand there a limitation to what he can do - but he must do something; correct? He must respond in some manner. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in the next sentence you say: "This" -- the duty to act or to do something "does not mean that officers can be held responsible for the particular behaviour or actions of soldiers or not under their direct command and over whom they have no direct influence." So if I understood that correctly - and tell me if I have - all the commanders have a duty to act or do something if they are aware of a breach of discipline by someone who is not within their own unit; you're saying they're not responsible for that specific behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I can give an example if you like or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... can just --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say that's true. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's clear to me, but if the Chamber wants you to go further, I'll give them an opportunity to do so. But to me it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And now so -- and the commander that has a duty to do something regarding a breach of discipline by someone who is not in their unit, although they are not responsible for that behaviour, can they be held responsible if they did not take any action with respect to that breach?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used the word "commander," and, really, this is a -- something that every officer has to be aware of. Now, you will say to me quite rightly, all officers are commanders. In fact, they're not, because some officers are doing staff jobs; they commands nothing. But all officer have a responsible -- responsibility if they see or hear of - and this is -- this is almost inevitably after the fact - if they see of or hear of a breach of discipline in terms of behaviour normally - and normally these are trivial issues - then they have a responsibility to do whatever they can to enable that offender, the alleged offender to be brought to book. Now, whether that is stopping the offence, will you not do that, or whether that is reporting it to the superior, that person's superior, or whether it is merely passing it on, I saw this happen, can you please make sure that somebody knows about this, will depend upon all sorts of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When I make pauses that might seem unusually long to you, it's simply for the translations.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Not because I'm questioning any of your answer. So -- and you said that typically are trivial issues -- trivial breaches if they were more serious breach, the same obligation on - and I accept your correction - on all officers would say be the same; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just for the record you need to --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I'm -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about the officers - and I'll try to use the correct term because that is the one you used in your report as well - you talked about officers being responsible for the behaviour of their subordinates for any breaches of discipline, you used the term "and" meaning that to be responsible, in your view, they must both be under, first, the command of the superior, and, secondly, the commander, or the officer must be able to excerpt direct influence over that subordinate. Only one of the two would not be sufficient. Is that your view characterised accurately? I'm reading from page 10 in your --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I'm just reading it again. "And over whom they have no direct..." I mean, command gives you authority, enables you one -- there is -- there is no authority without the -- the -- the capacity to sanction. Authority is about essentially making people do things, imposing your will upon people. And that can be done in many ways, but the final way of doing it is by the threat of sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you say that that is limited by those two factors, that is based on your experience of the United Kingdom and NATO, general rules of discipline; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, could I seek one point of clarification. On page 10, you're referring to behaviour as breaches of military discipline. Was it your intention to limit it to the -- well, let's say, disciplinary breaches or also more serious misbehaviour, such as crimes committed in the course of ... I'm just trying to find out, because sometimes you say that this does not mean that officers can be held responsible for the particular behaviour or actions of soldiers, where you do not make any distinction between what kind of ill behaviour. Whereas sometimes you refer to undisciplinary behaviour and - I would say crimes is certainly not disciplinary behaviour. So -- but I did not -- I do not know whether you wanted to include that in this section which is under the general heading of authority and responsibility of a commander, or whether you would exclude that from what you wrote here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, breaches of military discipline, of course, can be very serious, as you well understand, Your Honour. I think if you use the word crime in general in terms of civil crime, not being a lawyer, I would have difficulty saying that -- that my -- my overall view that officers have a responsibility to deal with crime, I don't think that is true, because I think there are elements of the criminal law which firstly they do not have a responsibility for are immediately matters pertaining to the civil police. And in some cases they will have no understanding that a crime has been committed. I mean, it could be something like fraud, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you don't know, of course, you can't respond to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least or unless there is a situation where you should have known. But I'm just trying to figure out whether -- I do understand the -- the reservations you make. But if, in the course of the exercise of military duty, a crime, which could be, just theoretically speaking, could be a war crime or attacking a civilian person or -- would that fall outside the scope of what you describe here, or would it be part of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would form -- it would fall inside that scope. Attacking a civilian person is a military crime as well as a civil one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just seeking clarification of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- scope of what you describe on page 10 under subparagraph (c). Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just in line with that clarification, would the -- a crime as well fall under the scope of the duty of an officer to do something if he was aware of it happening if that soldier is not under his direct command?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is reported to an officer it becomes apparent, through whatever means, that something has been done wrong, whether it is a trivial -- relatively trivial disciplinary incident or whether it is a more serious crime, he actually has to take some action to ensure that the alleged incident is dealt with, is investigated, is -- yeah. Is investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And just staying -- or going back to what we were discussing before based on -- this is it based on your experience and knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- as a very senior officer. I take it, sir - and I don't mean to -- I just have to ask you this question - but I take it you were not aware of this Tribunal's jurisprudence under Article 7(3) of its Statute dealing with command responsibility and the liable -- and the criminal responsibility of superior officers for their acts of their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have actually heard it quoted, but I wouldn't be familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
