utterances.text: And similarly, I take it, you would not know the specific requirements in this Tribunal's jurisprudence on that -- on that issue; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I've heard it talked about, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, similarly, on Friday, Mr. Cayley showed you some portions -- or, read out some portion of the indictment to you and asked you for your comments on those. In those passages, the words "effective control" were mentioned. Were you aware that those words have a very specific meaning, legal meaning, given to them by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware there is a specific legal meaning in those word, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But when you were providing your answers or comments to the questions from Mr. Cayley, you were not referring to those specific words as a -- as -- as their legal meaning. We were talking about generally about your understanding of General Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm sure we shall get on to the other point at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We most definitely will. You also note at page 11 of your report this time, the last paragraph: "For there is a substantial part played by non-commissioned officers, ultimately, it is officers who are responsible for creating and sustaining good order and, as such, they must, at all times, maintain good order and military discipline, however personally difficult it may be." Could you please just elaborate on that briefly for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, it -- the only reason you have officers with their particular constitutional position is to -- we use the phrase "they are the morale guardians of -- of the service." They are responsible for setting the example. The example officers set is the example seen by soldiers and, of course, this is picked up very clearly and very -- I think, in a very positive way by the old JNA doctrine, in terms of leadership. So officers do bear a responsibility in -- in -- in all the armies I have ever been involved in. And they are supported by non-commissioned officers. But the non-commissioned officers, take their lead from the commissioned officers. It is the commissioned officer who is are responsible for setting -- as General Pringle very interestingly uses the phrase, "command climate."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we will get to command climate in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I thought it was over, but it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just, at page 12 lines 18 to 20, I think you address, at least in part, the Presiding Judge's clarification, and you say: "It is the duty of all officers to ensure that breaches of discipline, whether major or minor, are properly reported to the relevant authority." That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's -- let's turn now to - which we seem to be on the same page - to command climate, which is the a page 13 of your report, where you discussed the importance for a commander to establish a strong command climate. And that's at lines 28 and following. You state: "It is the prime responsibility of officers and entirely dependant upon the examples they set, the clarity with which they explain and justify the standards that must be met and their determination to compel, when necessary, adherence to those standards." General, if a -- if an officer or a commander does not discipline his subordinates for breaches of military discipline, whether minor or major, what impact would that have on the command climate?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the failure to discipline breaches of military discipline will normally lead, normally lead to a reduction from standards of discipline. It doesn't inevitably do so. And, indeed, I have to say that, at times, not disciplining some -- somebody, there may be a justification for it. But that is unusual. And that is part of the very very complex relationship that exists between officers and men and the rest. But, in general term, you're right. It will lead to a reduction in the standard of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what impact would failure to discipline or take action against crimes committed by soldiers, what impact would that have on the command climate?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could encourage other soldiers to believe that they do not have to obey orders themselves. And I think we need to be careful here also, that there is a -- a sense that a soldier does nothing unless he is given an order to do something. This is not what we're talking about. This is the acceptance of -- this is the -- the I'm sorry -- this is the carrying out of -- of those essential duties of a soldier which are -- should be well known and should be done without anybody having to give an order. This is the -- the daily standards of -- of discipline, care for your equipment, treating people decently, doing that which you know to be right without anybody supervising you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that I follow you. Would it be fair to say that failing to punish crime or failing to discipline troops who committed crimes is likely to create a climate that would encourage others to commit crimes as well?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would use the word "encourage." It depends how you use it. It will certainly -- it may certainly reduce the -- the innate obedience to regulation and discipline in other people. Now, whether that is encouragement or not is another issue. But it does lead to a decline in the efficiency and effectiveness of force, because can you not trust the people are do things they should be doing without being supervised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I accept your clarification. Could the same be said about officers who fail to take action with respect to the failure -- sorry, let me restate that. Could the same be said about officer who failed to respond in some manner to either breaches of discipline or crimes which you've mentioned earlier they are required to do in some way. Would that also likely affect the command climate?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: These offences that affect the command climate are more likely to be the -- the -- the essentially trivial ones, the ones about behaviour, ones about maintaining standards, cleaning weapons, ensure vehicles are properly serviced. It is that which starts to eat away at the effectiveness of the unit. It doesn't lead to breakdowns in discipline, in terms of increasing violence or -- necessarily. And that is specifically what I'm talking to in terms the commands climate. It is -- command climate is all about the attitude soldiers have to their soldiering and their willingness, their willingness, to do that which they should do without being supervised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Perhaps it was my mistake in the question, and I do accept that. Leaving command climate as a specific term aside, would the fact that a soldier committed a crime and that he was not disciplined in any manner, would that make it more likely that others will also commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You use the word "crime." And I would prefer to use the word "breaches" of discipline because I think crime has a -- we already discussed with the Chamber the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Maybe, just for the purposes of these questions, we can just find a -- find way -- I'm talking about -- well, you said, attacking a civil for example would be both a crime and a --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And -- and a breach of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Destroying civilian property or disregarding civilian property would be both a breach of discipline and a crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Those are the ones that I'm talking about. I'm talking about crimes, you know, like fraud or -- like -- those are the crimes I'm discussing.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about that sort of crime, violence against somebody, then the absence of legal action against one soldier may not have any effect. But if it's a common trend that commanders do not impose sanctions upon those soldiers that commit these offences, as a matter of course, then those soldiers who are subordinated to them, as a matter of course, then, of course, it can lead to a -- a further breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, similarly, would it be the same if those breaches of discipline/crimes, when they're not people under their -- under their direct command but for whom they have an obligation to respond in some way -- be it reporting to the authorised person or whatever, would that also have the same possible effect, if it kept on happening?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think, in the way that we are painting. Remember, the command climate is the responsibility of the officer who has soldiers subordinated to him. If you take somebody who observes an incident and fails to report it because he is travelling in a car and -- and can't do anything and then forgets it, that, in itself, I don't think, would be -- create the sort of situation that you have -- have you suggested. So the -- the -- the most important element in this is the element of a superior officer and a subordinated soldier, soldiers, that is the relation -- that is where the relationship really exists. The rest are very much more peripheral, the impact of the rest is very much more peripheral.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And drawing on your experience, if a commander or an officer has troops directly subordinated to him this time, so in the direct chain, that have committed crimes in a prior operation and those crimes have not been addressed in any way, would it make it more likely that the same soldiers or others in that unit would go on to another operation shortly after would also commit similar crimes?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a reasonable position to take. Whether it's backed up in fact is another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Based on your experience commanding a large number of officers, it would be likely - would it not? - that failing to take action against someone who committed something that was a crime, and then sending him out the next day or two days later without telling him that he should not do that, that he will -- he is more likely to do it again than if he was told not to, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the -- that's the reasonable assumption to make from there, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now let's go one step further. If a commander, prior to an operation, issues a specific order to his soldiers not to commit certain actions, if, despite these order, these soldiers in fact commit these actions, if they are not disciplined and that these same soldiers that are used in an operation shortly thereafter, what would you, as a commander, do, to make sure that those same actions would not take place? Would you issue the same orders or simply say something else?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking generally here are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At this stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, it goes back to the essential point that I made. If in any particular unit it is seen that orders can be disobeyed without sanction, then there will be a sense that this is fair enough and we will continue to do that. That is a general principle which I think falls out of everything that we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry if my questions sometimes may seem obvious to you. I don't have the same expertise as you have on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope my answers are clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking myself, Mr. Hedaraly, to what extent this expert witness has knowledge on how troops would behave in the future, if crime or undisciplined behaviour occurred and if nothing was done, I do not know whether the expert witness ever experienced such a situation or not, not on, perhaps, on a mass scale but on a large scale, undisciplined behaviour was not responded to in any way, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am very fortunate I have never experienced that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, that doesn't come fully as surprise to me. And, Mr. Hedaraly, you are certainly aware that the effect of imposing sanctions and what would happen if you do not impose sanctions and what the effect is if you do impose sanctions, is -- is a matter which, I take it from the previous answer of this expert witness, is only to a limited extent a field in which he has experienced or whether he is -- has some specific expertise. And I think for all the lawyers in this courtroom, it's clear that the effect of imposing sanctions is a matter over which we have hot debates already for, well, one century or two centuries. So, therefore, I would invite you to remain as focussed as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can have on the screen 65 ter 2D00567. General, this is one of the documents you've referenced in your report. It is the report of General Pringle. And at page 15 line 15 of your report, when you are discussing the command climate, you said that it was well described by General Pringle. I just wanted to ask you if the sections that you reviewed are the appropriate paragraphs that I want to show you which are at page -- page 10 starting at paragraph 38. But before I ask you my question, I notice that my learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to give you an opportunity to finish your question before -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting. Obviously this is a report for an expert that the Prosecution did not call. There are a number of facets to this report, and reading the report I understand why he was not called. That being said, before we get too far down the road with this report, with some attempt on the part of the Prosecution to admit it, I'd like some order of proof coming from the Prosecution as to what they intend to do. If there's going to be some type of addressing or putting a portion of this report into evidence, frankly it's a violation of Rule 94 bis. So the reason I rise at this point, Mr. President, because I do believe that -- well, I should say that I suspect that we will be going down that road and we will have an objection because the Prosecution chose not call General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to make clear, I do appreciate the issue and I do appreciate that is an expert who the Prosecution has not called and therefore was not cross-examined by -- by the Defence. However, it is a report that is specifically referred to by this expert. It is a report that he therefore concludes is one of the key documents that helped him reach the conclusions in his report. He essentially says that he has adopted at least one portion of it, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So the situation is the following. The report says, I read X and it is well described. And I'm now repeating it here. Whereas X itself is nowhere on the record. Now, the only alternative is for me to read out that portion on the record and ask the expert if that's what he was with referring to. And, although I do appreciate the situation about the fact that he was not called by the Prosecution, the fact of the matter remains that that report was relied on by this expert. And I'm happy to ask him which portions he relied, did he review the whole report, what did he think of it. But, otherwise, we don't have anywhere, in terms of transparency, which portions were relied on. We have a footnote generally describing the report. And even in his testimony today, the witness referred to General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You made an objection. Mr. Hedaraly has responded. Your objection is denied, Mr. Kehoe. What follows in the following questions is still to be seen. This expert witness apparently has been provided with a report, which he considered, I take it from his point of expertise, relevant. He quoted it. Under those circumstances, Mr. Hedaraly is at least entitled to put questions to him. Whatever the follow-up may be, we do not know yet, all of the questions. So, therefore, the objection against putting this question to the witness is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, when you were describing the -- in your report, the description of the command climate, and when you said it was well-described by Major-General Pringle, if you look on your screen, and if we can go page by page until page 13 until the end of that section. Can you just confirm for us that that was the section that you relied upon when you made that statement in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The section that starts with question 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did. I mean, I read the whole of the Pringle report, but I looked particularly at question 5 and used the answers to that question to inform my -- my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you essentially agreed with Major-General Pringle's conclusions in that section?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed with what he said, yes. I -- there was one conclusion which we may come to which I felt he overstated, but we might discuss that. I ought to say, for transparency, that General Pringle is a personal friend of mine, and that we were at Sandhurst together and worked together on one or two occasions. And he knows that I'm doing what I'm doing, and I know that he obviously -- and he knows that I know that he wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to -- just do maybe cut matters short, can you tell us which one was the conclusion that you disagreed with? Is it at the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, this document is not yet in evidence. So, therefore, to put the question to the witness whether he agrees with what General Pringle said doesn't give any evidentiary value. I allowed you to put questions to this expert witness in relation to General Pringle's report, but if it is not in not in evidence, then any comparison is totally useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say, You have written down this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from -- of course, you can ask the witness whether he ever experienced any disagreement with what he read as conclusions of General Pringle. Then what we would then known is, first of all, what General Pringle, apparently, on that item, said and that this expert witness disagreed with him in this respect. Now, for the others, whether or not anything more should be in evidence or not, apparently you're not seek this report to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that was the guidance I was seeking, Mr. President. The witness now has explicitly stated that he relied on four pages of those. And I understand they're not on the record. So it seems the only option is either that it gets an exhibit number so that we know what the witness is referring to, or I read those four pages which is going to take quite a long time so that we have it on the record. And that was -- that's the guidance that I was seeking earlier. I can put a few other questions to the witness, but then how do we deal with the matter so that everyone does have the right information on the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, but, of course, what I see is Major-General Pringle in his report. I then see 65 ter and then the number. That's everything we know. Then you know, of course, the case law, that if documents are produced for the purposes of this proceedings, I do not know whether that's the case or not, because I have got no information whatsoever about it. The only thing I see now, Q 5 on the screen, but could you tell us more, then, about the report. Apparently it has been -- I don't know been provided by who. Perhaps by Mr. Cayley to the expert witness. Mr. Cayley may have considered it to be relevant for the witness to learn about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. The report was provided to the witness at a time when the Defence believed that Major-General Pringle was going to be a witness in the case. Subsequently, for whatever reason, the Prosecution decided not to call Major-General Pringle. But, of course, General Deverell had written his report and had considered the matters that General Pringle had set out in his report. But I think, you know, you've already pointed out - you've referred to the case law - to now use that as a vehicle to somehow get in through the back door -- Major-General Pringle's report, well he never gave evidence before this Chamber, I think would be improper. And the better way to do it would simply be to cross-examine on the basis of the report and asked about the principles reflected there. Otherwise, what's happening in essence is that the expert report is going in without the expert witness ever having given evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make I take it that you join Mr. Cayley' position, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you have got approximately one hour's time to consider the present situation because we will have a lunch break. Of course, you can further discuss it. But, procedurally, now knowing that this was an expert report which was prepared for the purposes of this proceedings, from what I understand, an expert report of a witness who finally was not called by the Prosecution may create some problems. I would like you to consider that. We'll have a break, and we will resume at a quarter to 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, first of all, we'll -- this afternoon's session, we'll first go on until quarter past 4.00 and then resume at 25 minutes to 5.00, and then continue until 6.00. If that's clear. Then I gave you an hour to consider certain matters. Have you made up your mind? Does it change anything in your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It does, Mr. President, I will follow my learned friend Mr. Cayley's suggestion and simply go through a few of the matters in the report and examine the witness and not seek to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, you -- you stated you had reviewed General Pringle's report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's already on the screen. I will just go through a few portions, a few paragraphs, and simply ask you whether you agree with him or not and if there are any additional comments that you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can first go to page 5 at paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is under the heading: List and discuss the main principles that universally apply to command and control in armed forces in the world, including the HV. Now there will be some overlap between your report and this one, but I just want to make sure that the discussion is the same. So paragraph 17 says: "Command refers to the authority vested in an individual for the direction, coordination, and control of military forces. It therefore encompasses the authority, responsibility, and duty to act. Leadership and decision making describe the commander's primary responsibilities. Command also involves accountability and control." General, do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the Chamber would prefer if you would first try to explore where this witness disagrees with yet an unknown portion of a report which is not in evidence and then you can elicit whatever you want where apparently the witness is in agreement with Mr. Pringle. And then you just ask him about it. And you know that it's consistent with Mr. Pringle's position, and we do not know but we do not have to know because it is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, do you remember which conclusion of Mr. Pringle you disagreed with?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could scroll down the -- the page, please. I think it's over the next page. I'm sorry, I haven't got General Pringle's report to hand, only the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember what section it was in?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, frankly. It was end -- if you look at the end of question 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's go to the end of question 5, which is paragraph 13, I believe -- page 13. If you can go to the top of that page, right there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, it's the end, I think, of question 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be paragraph 53. Or 52, perhaps if we can scroll down the screen from the beginning so that the General can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's not there. Please keep going down. Keep going down. Hmm. Perhaps you can try the next page. I'm sorry I'm not being able to find. I know precisely what I'm looking for; I just can't remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, let me suggest the following. At the next break we will provide with you a hard copy --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I think that would be much better, yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you can look at it and let us know if you --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a -- it's a very small issue, and it is a -- it's not a disagreement of the statement; it's an interpretation which -- a different interpretation that I would put upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because, Mr. Hedaraly, this witness appears as an expert witness before us, to what extent he disagrees with others is -- well, if it's like, I read this in literature and I disagree with this author is, of course, for an expert, appropriate to tell us. But this seems to be very much focussed on this case and therefore to what extent he agrees or disagrees is not -- we do understand that it's only on one point that the witness disagrees whatever he wants to tell us is in the report. Whatever you'd like to add to that and whether or not to be found in a report authored by Mr. Pringle seems not to be a relevant issue for us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I do understand the guidance, Mr. President. It's simply because the witness has relied on this -- on this specific document to come to his conclusions. He -- it's one of the key documents he relied on, and that was the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I see is command climate well described by Major-General Pringle. So the only thing I find here, but -- is that he says, Well, that person, what I considered to be right, is well-described by him. Which, of course, whether that's relying on someone else or just saying, Well, someone else who has a similar position described it well. That's -- if we -- yes, of course, there are other portions where more is described. But he then describes that again in a certain way, and let's -- let's try to avoid that this witness is telling us what General Pringle wrote in his report. Even if he relies on it to some extent, then ask him similar questions or to the extent relevant and not appearing in this report, but let's try not to -- to make it a kind of a twin report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, under this score, going into issues even that Mr. -- that General Deverell disagreed with is indirectly putting this report in when he is not relying on that aspect of the report. Now, if the cross-examination wants to explore those citations in General Deverell's brief that cites General Pringle, I think that we can go through that through the exercise of pointing out that portion of the report or General Pringle's report upon which General Deverell relies. But to go into what he disagrees with is outside that which General Deverell relied upon in order to formulate his report. And what we have in evidence is the report, not those portions upon which there may have been a departure of opinion. So we would disagree that getting into some exercise where we went into facets that upon which these two Generals disagreed is appropriate. I submit to you, Mr. President, it's not appropriate and that our focus should be on those portions cited by General Deverell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I have consulted my colleagues. The Chamber does not agree with you. Where the witness said that it's only one point that he disagreed with what Mr. Pringle has written, again, which is not in evidence, that means that it could be a matter - and I do understand it's not a major thing; it's just interpretation of a certain matter - the Chamber would like to know then also what the other interpretation would have been so that we are better able to assess the value of what this expert witness tells us. But it may be clear to you as well that the Chamber is certainly trying to avoid that we have two for the price of one. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, if local troops drawn from an area where they were racial tension or ethnic conflict previously who were involved in an operation, that would be something that a commander would take into account; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it -- I'm sorry. Yes, he should be taking it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if such troops had to be involved in an operation, the commander would have a special responsibility to ensure that they conducted themselves properly?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, yes, he does. Realistically, it's very much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I say in my report that actually sometimes you find, particularly in the sort of environment we're talking about, locally-raised forces' loyalty is greater to their local commanders than to their more senior commanders who maybe do not come from that local area. And I experienced this myself in -- in Northern Ireland. So there is -- there is a realistic issue here about exactly how that level of command and control is achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fair enough. What I'm trying to get at is that the commander would be conscious of that and would make or should make more efforts than usual to at least try to control his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he should make every effort he needs to make to ensure that his soldiers behave properly. How much effort that requires will depend upon the standard of training of the soldiers he has under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to -- actually, I forgot to ask you before when we were discussing the general process by which you prepared your report. You told us on Friday that you had prepared a draft initially and that that draft had been modified, that you eliminated some duplication, and that you eliminated portions dealing with Grubori. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a draft. It was a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And as such --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, to finish off, to answer your question, yes, I did make certain changes, one of which involved Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But that was a report -- so that was a report that you were happy to have submitted before you were told that it could be presented more efficiently, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would you be willing to provide a copy of that report to the Court, to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've got a particular copy. It's on -- it was brought together as a -- you know, a group of separate elements, and I think the only -- the only copy may well be, you know, within the Cermak Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And would you be willing to look for it electronically?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going object to this point because this matter has already been addressed by the Court. I can't recall the exact day, but I recall your words, which were, Drafts are not to be provided and that these matters can be explored in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was a disclosure obligation of the Defence team. I'm asking the witness directly if he's willing to provide us a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cayley, I'm -- I must say that one of the previous answers was: "It was not a draft. It was a report." Therefore, if you're referring to what should be done with drafts, then that answer would not fully support your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, what I'm -- the point I'm making is that Mr. Hedaraly know's what the legal position is, and I think to be asking the witness that question is improper in light of the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would simply refer also that the Court did ask Mr. Theunens directly, without asking the Prosecution whether they had any objections. And then when the witness agreed, it was on an invitation of the Court. I'm simply making a similarly invitation to the witness, and if he is happy with that report, I see no reason why I cannot ask the witness directly if he is willing to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the Chamber understood that you wanted to invite Mr. Deverell to express his opinion on whether he would -- had any problems in making available to the Chamber the -- what I then understand is a Grubori part of the report which was finalised but then taken out because the report would be too extensive. Is that -- or not really the matter you wanted to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am -- I am to state the obvious, I'm the Court's servant here. I have nothing hide by trying to prevent people seeing what I had previously written in my report. It is up to the Court to decide. I would have difficulty -- I may have some difficulty being absolutely certain from my point of view, within my own system, exactly the report I sent because I have several copies of my draft, my drafts, which I put together. And it may be that if I put together that -- those drafts into what I thought was the report I sent in, there could be other issues which -- other -- other mistakes and things that I had rejected. So there is, from my point of view, a technical, a physical problem, from the point of view of the evidence -- I'm sorry the report, there is nothing in that report that I would not be able to, personally, to defend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider whether it will invite whomever that would be at the moment to -- to be provided with the Grubori chapter of the report. Is that how I could say it? Because you said it was a report, it was part of the report you submitted which was finalised and then it was -- that portion was taken out for very practical reasons. We will consider it, whether we will do that. And, at this moment, Mr. Hedaraly, you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, I want to now move to a -- the appointment of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And at page 8 of your report, I'm referring to lines 12 to 15, you state that there were three elements of Cermak's appointment to Knin. First, as a garrison commander; second, as an administrator to facilitate the normalisation of Knin; and, third, a point of contact for international organisations. Now, General, he was appointed to Knin for these three tasks by President Tudjman. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And President Tudjman was the head of state and Supreme Commander of the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And under the rules, he to appoint generals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you don't dispute President Tudjman's authority to make that appointment?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And will you agree with me that assisting with the normalisation of Knin did not come strictly within the tradition responsibilities of a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your report, in fact, you refer to that role with respect to normalisation at page 35 of your report where you discuss P1144, a transcript of a meeting between President Tudjman and General Cermak, where these tasks were described. And they included, among other things, keeping order, preventing disorders, infrastructure, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you remind me of the page? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Absolutely. 35.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 35, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's where you --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's where you describe the tasks associated with the normalisation, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And similarly being the point of contact of international organisation does not fall within the tradition roles of a garrison commander. I think you said --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was also a tasking that he received directly from President Tudjman, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe, to be semantic about this, that presidents give tasks. They give direction, strategic direction, I mean, the classic source, Supreme Commander and chief gives direction to the operational commander from which tasks are devolved. It's part of the planning process. So to say that was given a task by the president is -- is incorrect. He was certainly given direction as to what he should do. But that is not, I would suggest, a task in the accepted meeting -- meaning of a task not least because a task should have resources attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Maybe it's just semantics, but President Tudjman as the Supreme Commander, told General Cermak to deal with international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He directed him to do so. I -- I merely wanted to identify that we didn't uses the word "task" in a loose and general sense only to come back to it to refer to it in a very specific sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. And those -- and two of those functions, or however we call it, appointments of President Tudjman with respect to General Cermak, the normalisation of Knin and being the point of contact, did not fall within the tradition responsibilities of a garrison commander, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, since those responsibilities fell outside the traditional roles of a garrison commander and yet General Cermak was appointed to perform those tasks or responsibilities not to -- it would follow that his authority with respect to these issues would also come from sources outside the traditional sources of authority of a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does presuppose that there was any authority for him to carry out those tasks. I saw nothing in writing which gave him any authority to carry out those tasks. The only authority he had came from his -- his appointment as garrison commander. As far as could I see, I saw nothing which said, Here is this General who is officially employed to do these other two tasks. It was entirely a general direction from the Supreme Commander, President Tudjman, who used the position of a garrison commander in order to put him in place, in order to do, in my judgement, primarily the task of urban regeneration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Are you disputing President Tudjman's ability to -- or authority to appoint General Cermak to carry out functions with respect to normalisation of Knin and being the point of contact with international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not disputing his authority to say, I wish there to be a point of contact and I wish there to be somebody who goes to conduct urban regeneration; neither am I disputing his authority say, And, General Cermak, It should be you. But what I didn't see was anything which said, Here are the precise authorities you have. Here are the sanctions can you impose upon those who fail to comply with you in terms of fish farms, et cetera, et cetera. I didn't see anything which gave him any power to do what he actually did. Now, if there are documents that -- that do this, then -- or I have misinterpreted documents, then I would be very grateful to be shown them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Whether there are documents or not, all I'm trying to establish is that President Tudjman had that authority. Now, whether there is a document that we have here or not is not really my question. My question is: Did he have the authority to assign General Cermak to carry out those responsibilities. Right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that to be true. He did have the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you say that General Cermak's actual authority and responsibility were limited by his appointment, that of a garrison commander, that would mean that his authority and responsibility with respect to his appointment as garrison commander were limited by that, but we just don't know what the authority -- what the limitations, if any, were for the two other functions; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of no limitations for his authority for the other two functions because I know of no authority he ever had to do the other two functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So your position is that President Tudjman did not give him the authority to carry out the two other portions of his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he -- if we agree that authority consists of power to -- to -- to act, that people have to obey your instructions, I saw nothing which gave President Cermak [sic] the authority to start issuing instructions to banks or fish farms or -- or whatever. I saw nothing which gave him the authority to actually deal with the international communities. All he got was a general direction from President Tudjman to go and do it, and they placed him, as garrison commander, to give him what they thought was the wherewithal to do that job. Because there was no other appointment they could give him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned "general direction" a few times. Did you know that Mr. Cermak considered the task that he received from President Tudjman to amount to an oral order? That's how he referred to it.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- sorry, General Cermak may well have done. But I saw no evidence that he had, from that instruction, any authority. It is one thing to order somebody to -- to perceive somebody as ordered you to do something; it is another thing, I believe, then to take upon yourself the authority you need to comply with that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, General, if the Supreme Commander told Cermak to do something, and if Cermak thought that that was an order, wouldn't you agree with me that that's what he had to do?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree that that's what he had to do. I think we're mixing up my view of President Tudjman's authority to tell General Cermak to do something. I want you to go and sort out Knin and help the Canadians, I think, is a rough translation, a sort of contemporaneous translation of what he was told. That is what, I think, General Feldi said, if I remember correctly. That is very different from then giving the person you have given that instruction or getting your staff to find for that person the actual authority which enables you to do it. The legal basis upon which you issue instructions. And he only gave him the authority that came through the appointment of a garrison commander. And your authority comes from your appointment and not your rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if we accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if we accept General Cermak's view that he received an oral order, are you saying that President Tudjman gave him an order without giving him any means to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am. I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you don't know - do you? - what President Tudjman specifically told General Cermak as to what he could and what he could not do; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I wasn't in the room at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the fact that General Cermak was appointed by President Tudjman gave him a status that was different than those of other garrison commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Status can be used in two senses: legal status, or social status. I don't believe he gave him any legal status any more than that which the appointment of garrison commander afforded him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Because he was appointed by the Supreme Commander, the Main Staff, for example, were limited with respect to what they could or could not do with respect to that appointment; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all Generals were appointed by the Supreme Commander under the constitution. So, I mean, I'm not quite sure the point you're making there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the way in which you dealt with the matter until now, if you want to show the witness is any document is fine, then we'll move on. But the Chamber takes the position that, without any specifics in the way it was done, that the matter had be sufficiently explored. But if you want to go into any further details, then, of course, that would be a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just waiting for a number that I didn't write down.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Obviously my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 7466, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, General, there will be an order from the Main Staff coming up. You see it's dated 9 November, 1995. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we look under item one, it's an order from the Main Staff to eliminate the commands of garrisons.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We'll see -- we see under item four who essentially is now supposed to perform the duties of the garrison commanders. And various Military Districts are listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to page 4, we will see the list for the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you will see here that all the other garrisons within the Split Military District are listed: Split, Zadar, Sinj, Vrgorac, Imotski, Dubrovnik, and Benkovac. But that Knin is not listed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can now go to 65 ter 7467.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this will be a December 1995 clarification of this order that you will see. Just go to the bottom and you see it says: "Acting commanding officer for the Knin garrison was not designated in the order," and there is a description in the order which we have just seen, "because the Supreme Commander of the Croatian armed forces appointed General Cermak to the duty of the Knin garrison commanding officer, as per his order. The acting Knin garrison commanding officer will be appointed after the Supreme Commander's decision becomes invalid." Now, General, these two documents show that, because General Cermak was appointed directly by President Tudjman, that he had to be -- in some respects treated differently from other garrison commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was treated differently because he was a General. Therefore, you are right that if other garrison commanders were not Generals, then General Cermak is being treated differently. But he had to be appointed by the Supreme Commander, and, I guess, I would presume, that therefore he would have to be -- his appointment would have to be annulled at some stage by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's what this document says?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That it's because President Tudjman appointed him directly?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can tender 65 ter 7466 and 64 7467 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, those documents become Exhibit P2656 and P2657, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2656 and P2657 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, were you aware that General Cermak's appointment received media coverage both on television and in the printed media?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also state in your report that the garrison commanders are normally middle-ranking officer, major-colonels?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also refer to General Cermak as being over-ranked for the position.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would you agree, General, that the appointment of such a high-ranking person by the president could indicate that he wanted to make sure that his appointment got some attention among the military?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would say that it was clear that the -- the President wished to draw attention to the fact that he had put a senior officer down there, but I'm not sure it was your last couple of words, draw the attention of the military. I'm not sure I would agree with that. It don't think necessarily it follows. It may be -- it may that be you have a perfectly reasonable point. I would suggest that there is a perfectly reasonable alternatively that he was not seeking to impress the military; he was seeking to impress the wider Croatian public and the international community, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: My question was that it could be a sign of this. We don't know, obviously, but it could --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's perfectly reasonable to assume that. Its also, I would suggest, reasonable to assume that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fair enough. And this -- this an appointment was also special as we've discussed because it encompassed elements not traditionally associated with a garrison commander, and it was, therefore, a special appointment given to General Cermak at a very special time, right after Knin was liberated; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And Knin had a significant symbolic importance to Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you know that after his appointment General Cermak continued to communicate with the office of the president and even with the president himself?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe to be so, although there is little evidence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you aware that in his interview General Cermak stated that, in fact, he would deal directly with the office of the president on the issues of normalisation and contact with international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which interview was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I believe he said it in the 1998 and the 2001 interview. But I can get specific reference and show them to you --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this was an after-the-fact interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. An interview with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misheard that. Yes, yes. I was aware of that. I'm sorry. I thought it was a media interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: My question was open to confusion.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you are aware that he had said that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that he said it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you know that this Chamber has received evidence that, as far back as 1992, some people in the Main Staff thought that General Cermak was untouchable because he was believed to have immense power, given his close relationship with the president and the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that, but I've seen no evidence of it. And, from my point of view, that was -- as it were, gossip. And I took no notice of it. I haven't heard that specific phrase, but I knew there were people who were saying such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You have also indicated that General Cermak was, I think you said, uniquely to be a garrison commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, regardless of General Cermak's qualifications, he was still appointed as garrison commander and, therefore, had to carry out all the duties and responsibilities of a garrison commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if he failed in doing so, he would be responsible just as any other officer would have been?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could take that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me discuss briefly this issue of a military governor that has come up a few times. Now, you provided us with a definition, and it's also in your report. And if I understand correctly, and it was discussed again this morning, a military governor would be normally appointed in a country whose forces were operating in another country and there would be no civilian authority head in place. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in such a situation, the military governor would be the highest authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It would be a transitional period between the military operations that concluded and the establishment of civilian authority in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep. Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, were you aware, sir, that General Cermak himself stated on 11 August that there was no civil authority in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did he state that? I can't remember that specifically. Is that part of my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't know if it's part of your report, but we can look at it. It's D38.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I guess you're better with numbers than I am. It's an interview he gave to a media outlet. And we can see at the middle of the page, at the bottom of the screen now, right after the bolded portion, his response of what his task was. And then there is a sentence that said: "Currently, there is no civilian authority in Knin." That was according to General Cermak on the 11th of August. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were you aware that Mr. Pasic, who you mentioned, was highly ineffective, and therefore General Cermak was considered to have do everything and deal with all the problems?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that Mr. Pasic was removed in the early part of 1995 -- 1996. Whether he -- his ineffectiveness was apparent during this, on the -- is this the 11th August? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, what we have on the screen is 11th of August, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If his ineffectiveness was -- people were aware of his ineffectiveness, then I'm, you know, I'm not entirely certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, may I take it that what you are doing at this moment is to -- after you had asked the expert again about what he understood to be a military governor, to put together factual elements which would justify, or at least in the opinion of the Prosecution would justify, the two -- come to the conclusion that, referring to General Cermak as a military governor was not as wrong as many people said it was. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was what I was thinking, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is -- is not much assisted by that. The Chamber is aware of the terminology used. The Chamber is aware what the formal authority of a garrison commander was. The Chamber is aware of how this expert witness views the position of a -- of a military governor. And now, whether all the factual elements do fit or do not fit in or what caused the confusion, is not something that greatly assists the Chamber. Therefore, you're invited, if you have one more question, fine. But then please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand the guidance to be that the Prosecution's position that it may have been reasonable for others in the area to think that General Cermak had -- had powers similar to a military governor is sufficiently on the record. Have I understood the guidance of the Chamber correctly? Because otherwise I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or unreasonable. But all the factual elements are there. We know the formal positions. We know the definition of what a military governor is. And then, finally, what the importance is of this terminology. What -- that's -- because I feel that you more or less moved the witness into a direction that he, as an expert, would say, Well, it corresponds quite a bit with what I consider do be a military governor. That's -- to what extent it does fit or does not fit is -- the Chamber can explore that without further questioning on this matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record and the Chamber, I was simply doing that because that was an opinion given by the expert on that matter. It wasn't to unduly waste the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not -- I'm just giving the guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour. If we can move now to the authority of a garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you refer in your report more than once to the role of a garrison commander in maintaining good order and military discipline. For example, page 22, line 31: "The establishment and maintenance of good order and military discipline within a garrison is the principle task of a garrison commander and is more than just enforcing military discipline." You also say that at page 23, line 32: "A garrison commander is required to establish climate of good order and military discipline within a garrison." And I want to discuss the service regulations which are -- which is D34, which I know for a fact you're familiar with, because it is referenced in your report. And we'll go to Article 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sure that you have memorised Article 52 probably by now so we probably could start, but just so that everyone can follow --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be better if we had it on the screen, even though it's printed on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, D32. My mistake. I apologise, Mr. Registrar. It's D32. Mr. Registrar knows better than me what the exhibits are. If can you go to Article 52, please. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it states: "The garrison commander is responsible for placement, order, discipline, and service in the garrison. All units and institutions within the garrison are subordinate to the garrison commander in matters of order, discipline, and service." These are the service regulations. Now, I understand from your report that you seem to agree with the first sentence of Article 52 but not the second. Is that -- have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have tried to do is interpret the second, which I believe to be very ambiguous, and, if read literally, runs counter to Croatian doctrine, in terms of unity of command. The garrison commander can only be responsible for the discipline of those who are subordinated to him. But being a garrison commander and running a garrison whose task is to support the other parts of the army, he will have soldiers or units who are placed in his garrison. And what this is trying to do is to find a way through this apparent conflict between unity of command and good order. So his responsibility is only for those people who are subordinated to him and those who are making actual use of the -- what I would term garrison facilities and resources; plus, the other elements of good order, which might be as simple as speed limits which are laid down for the safety of other soldiers or for the safety of civilians in the garrison, which other soldiers who are not subordinated to him who may be transiting through the garrison, must obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that is your -- so you don't -- although the text of Article 52 suggests that all units within the garrison, that is, geographically within the garrison, are subordinate to the garrison commander in matters of order, discipline, and service. To you, that is not -- that is not a correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that -- my interpretation would be that they cannot be because that means that somebody who is driving a vehicle through the garrison from one point to another whilst he is in the garrison is somehow subordinated to the garrison commander and then is unsubordinated as he leaves the garrison. And I think that, in most armies, that would seem to be impractical. It revolves around the element of subordination which involves tasking. What this attempts to do, and if properly interpreted does do, and there are other -- there are other ways -- there are other methods they use to ensure this is so, what this attempts to do is prevent the garrison commander from having the authority to re-task soldiers or units, to re-task soldiers or units, who happen to be within the -- within the garrison boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, you said in your report that it would run afoul with the organisational order in that garrison commands do not have operational functions. You said that as well to Mr. Cayley, either this morning or Friday, that that's the problem, that the garrison commander does not have any operational tasks. And you just said that again today. General, nothing in Article 52 subordinates those units for operational purposes. It simply says they are subordinate to the garrison commander in matters of order, discipline, and service. There is nothing about operational subordination there, is there?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. But I have to focus on the order and discipline element because that is only pertaining to precise garrison issues, which could be, quite simply, ensuring that people obey the orders for when the fuel station is open, or when the eating facilities are open. It is -- it is simply to ensure good order within the garrison, so the garrison runs effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have just been told there may be a problem in the transcript at page 110, line 21. I asked you, General: "You will agree with me that assisting with the normalisation of Knin did not come strictly within the traditional responsibilities of a garrison commander." And the transcript is unclear. Could you please repeat your answer, whether you agreed or disagreed with that statement?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you -- I wasn't really concentrating, I am afraid. Could you just repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't think it's an issue in dispute, but I will read it to you again just so that the transcript is clearer. You will agree with me that assisting with the normalisation of Knin did not come strictly within the traditional responsibilities of a garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it did not come within the normal responsibilities of the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to Article 52. And I believe you -- yes, you just ran out the transcript, but you agree that there was nothing about operational subordination in Article 52; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it's dealt with earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At page 33 of your report, I have a few questions regarding lines 16 to 23, if you want to read that paragraph. And -- have you had a chance to review it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. You say the allegations of murder, looting, burning, and rape, et cetera, which were widely reported by UNCRO and other international organisations, and you go on. Can you tell this Chamber where you saw widely reported allegations of rape?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in the UNCRO reports, the Sector South reports. Did I say rape? I'm sorry. Well, I'm not sure. I did see one, and I recall, I did see one case of rape that was being actually dealt with. But certainly murder, looting -- murder, looting, and burning was the constant theme of the UNCRO reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So there were no wide allegations of rape in those reports?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that's my, rather loose, use of English there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine. Because if they have, I would have I would have liked to see them?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I'm -- I think I was warming to my task, I'm afraid, in describing things. That was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also stated that crimes such as burning and looting are of such a seriousness that the punishments available under Article 10 and 11 of the Code would clearly be inappropriate and inadequate, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, that is my -- that is my -- that is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was just pausing for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also hold it as self evident that such claims like looting and burning constitute major violations of discipline; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, do you know - I'm not asking about your views on the matter - but do you know whether burning and looting were considered as minor or major violations of the disciplinary code in 1995 in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no that I found when I looked through the military law documents. I found no specific reference to those two crimes. I -- I maid a presumption, which I would have -- would suggest was a reasonable presumption, that they were so serious that they would have been a major violation in that all the minor violations that were detailed in the -- the disciplinary code were what I would understand as minor violations. Within my own army, burning and looting would be a major criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We'll get into the Code of Military Discipline in more detail in a few minutes. But just to foreshadow that discussion, minor breaches of military discipline, according to the Code of Military Discipline of the HV, would be dealt with disciplinary measures and serious violation would say be dealt with disciplinary sentences. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we look at -- let me pull up for you P1008. That is not in your report. I don't know whether have you seen it or not, but we can take a look. And will you see here, General, a series of disciplinary measures that were reported by Major-General Krsticevic. Can you tell us if you remember seeing this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So it may have been in the collections provided to you; it may not have been, you just can't tell?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been I looked at the date and thought that's quite later on and it may have been covering things that I felt had been covered before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to page 9 in the English. And it's page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You will see here in the -- you will see that this gentleman has a disciplinary measure for failing to prevent a soldier of his platoon from setting haystacks on fire. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page. There is another disciplinary measure for setting fires on -- fire on haystacks. So these -- these offences were considered at the time as minor breaches of military discipline; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been a minor breach.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, if we go to P1007, which is the Code of Military Discipline, Article 26 of that Code gives garrison commanders the authority to issue such disciplinary measures. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You can wait for it come up on the screen, if you want; although you may know it from your report. So it says, let me just read it for the record: "Commanders of units, institutions, and garrisons ... shall issue disciplinary measures to offenders who are not members of their organic unit if such measures are necessary and required for maintaining order and discipline." I'm sorry I don't know if have you answered.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You said yes already, so ...

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At page 24 of your report, you state: "The garrison commander had the authority to deal with soldiers from non-organic units who were accused of minor violations relating specifically to the use and behaviour within garrison facilitates."

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
