utterances.text: Now, looking at Article 26 which is still on the screen, there is nothing there limiting the application of Article 26 for garrison commanders to the "use of and behaviour within garrison facilities." Is there?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the whole point of Article 26 is that it allows him to impose disciplinary measures on those who commit -- offences, mild -- or mild violations of the military code whilst using garrison facilities. And if we could go back -- Could we go back to the previous document because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Actually, I just first want to --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... fine. Okay. I'd like to go back and comment, if I may, if I'm allowed to, I'd like to go back and comment on that document because there is a point that I think needs to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's no problem at all. If you don't have a chance to do it now, you can always ask at the end of your examination if you feel something has been left out or that you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really think, if the witness is asking him to comment on a prior document, he has a comment to make now, then he should be allowed to do so now, as opposed to directed questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, within limited -- do a limited extent, witnesses, if they want to add something, they should not be referred to the end of their testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would just like to finish on this document first, and then we can go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's fair. If the comment is not specifically on the last question, and on this document ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a more general one, Your Honour, and I'm very happy to -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll finish with the document and then you have an opportunity to give your further comments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, all I am pointing out to you, General, is that there nothing in the language of Article 26, as it appears in front of you now, that talks about the use of facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We can go back to the last document. Was it the series of disciplinary measures that you wanted to comment on, or was it service regulations?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the details of -- of the two soldiers who had been charged with offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would you like to see it again or just comment?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure. It was P1008. And it was page -- pages 9 and 10. Just say when you are done with the first page, go to the second, and then, when you are done, let us know.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, of course, what we see here is a disciplinary measure having been awarded by the chain of command, which is entirely proper. That's what should have happened, because they were part of the 4th Guards Brigade, part of an operational unit. And, therefore, it is for the chain of command to investigate and deal with that, because there has to be, in a crime, I would suggest, a time and a place and the sort of crime, rather than just a general view that crimes had been committed. And quite clearly, here is somebody was accused and found guilty of doing something. My second point, if I may, is that you gave the impression, understandably, that setting haystacks on fire was burning. Well, it is. But if you look -- I think it's the second page, the second charge sheet -- sorry, not charge sheet, the second page of this, it says, Set three haystacks on fire, located in the vicinity of the house where members of the engineering company were accommodated. What we don't know is the context of this. You and I probably know that these haystacks that you find in Yugoslavia are quite small ones. They're small bundles. And it could well have been, I don't know, and I guess nor do you, that this was done either by negligence or accident. And what he's done, actually, he's being charged with endangering the lives of his own soldiers, rather than burning haystacks in order to deprive the farmer of that hay. I don't know that to be true, but I think it is -- I would suggest it is a reasonable assumption on the basis that had it been anything else, it probably would not have been seen as a minor violation. And the deduction -- I'm sorry, the punishment would probably have been greater than that. Now, I'm merely saying, Mr. Hedaraly, that there is another interpretation that you could make of that particular document. And finally, the final point, is that although Article 26 does not specify the use of facilities, it flows from Article 52 which does specify the use of facilities. So I believe there is a consistency there between 26 and 52 even though 26 doesn't actually specify it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, I hope I did not give the impression that I was unwilling to hear any of your explanations.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So don't feel you have to race through everything. You know, we can address the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- matters that come up.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wish to make -- make sure I have had the opportunity to make the point. Thank you for allowing me to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course. And I want to take some of the things you mentioned in turn because you said a lot of things and I want to make sure they dont get lost in the transcript. You provided some potential rationale for why those disciplinary measures occurred. And if we -- let's just look at the document on the screen, it says rationale. And you suggested that it was endangering own soldiers. But there it says the aforementioned person breached the military discipline by acting against the order and thus he damaged the reputation of the Croatian army. So you're right, I don't know the full context, but that's what the document says. Now, you -- then you went to Article 26 and Article 52 of the service regulations, and -- well let's -- you said that Article 52 talked about the uses of garrison facilities. It does not. That's your interpretation of Article 52 that reads in the use of the facilities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely true. That is my interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So let's go back to Article 26 now, because I want to make sure we don't get confused here between what the regulations say and what your interpretation of them are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have P1007 again on the screen. Article 26 again, which is page 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, in fact, General, Article 26 does not refer to uses -- to -- to the uses of garrison facilities as we've just discussed. That's something that you have read into Article 26. In fact, Article 26 is a: "General disciplinary power given to the commander of any unit, institutions, or garrison to discipline anyone if such measures are necessary and required for maintaining order and discipline." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, you can -- you can read it, Article 26, in isolation. But it is interesting, I would suggest, as to why you have to have -- why there is an Article 26. And I would suggest you have to read back to Article 52 because you have this complex relationship between the support of by the garrison -- I'm sorry, I'll rephrase that. The -- the required support of the operational army by garrisons, in terms of the provision of facilities, whether it be accommodation, whether it be laundry, whether it be fuel. And the -- the commander of that garrison has to have the authority to ensure that soldiers from non-organic units that are not formally -- formally subordinated to him, obey the simple rules which may be the opening times of fuel stations. And that is -- that is it my connection between the -- that is my view of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You've said that before, and I understood you the first time. All I am pointing out is that Article 52 does not say "use of garrison facilities." Your interpretation of Article 52 say it. We can have it on the screen if you want.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't use the word facilities, but it uses placement, order, discipline, and services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And Article 26 here talks as well about order and discipline. And all I am telling you is that Article 26, in fact, is the disciplinary power given to any commander. As it says: "Any unit, institution, and garrison to issue disciplinary measures to offenders who are not members of the organic unit." Right? And in that sense, I would suggest to you that it does not violate the principle of unity of command because it does not concern an operational matter but, rather, underscores the importance of maintaining order and discipline.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on one hand, you said it -- it gives him the chance to impose disciplinary measures on anybody. And then you said it doesn't influence operational matters. But, of course, it would do, because the -- one of the importance of a unity of command is precisely that, that the chain of command shall be entirely responsible for the discipline of those soldiers subordinated do it. And, therefore, I think that is -- this is a support measure. This does not -- this is an article which supports rather than cuts across. It enables people in particular situations to deal with this complex area where you have soldiers subordinated to other units, working, doing things within your own facilities, properly for a temporary period, down to a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, I understand the balance between ensuring proper discipline and the unity of command within, for example, a garrison. But if we look at Article 26, the second sentence, there is a mechanism there where the disciplinary measure issued to someone not from the same organic unit must be passed on to the offender's superior officer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And Article 26 does -- does two other things. Firstly, it implies that the garrison commander or the institutional commander must know that an offence has been committed, and that he is able to actually deal with the offenders, because he has no investigative powers for investigating somebody who has -- is not part of his unit, as I understand it; and secondly, it implies that he has the discretion not to take such measures but has to inform the offender's superior officer in the event of an offence being committed. So, in fact, he is -- he is dealing with his responsibility to ensure that offence is reported or dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the whole point of Article 26 is to deal with disciplinary matters of members that are not under the direct chain of command of the person, whether it be the unit, institution, or garrison. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we turn the page, to go over to the second paragraph of Article 26. If a garrison commander - and I'm just using an example; it could be any unit commander - decides that it is not necessary for someone that is not in his unit to be punished immediately, he may instead forward the matter to the offender's immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, surely that is not a violation of the principle of unity of command; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a violation of the principle of unity of command. In fact, it underscore it is. Because it is it the -- the unit's commander, the commander of the soldier who is subordinated to that unit, who deals with that incident, rather than somebody from outside his chain of command. It is merely -- it is purely reported to him the incident and the details of the incident, the evidence that is required to see the offence dealt with, it's merely reported to the superior officer by the person who has identified the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this, in fact, is a illustration of what we discussed earlier about the duty of any officer, if he witnesses a breach of military discipline, that he must take some action either if he is allowed to discipline -- deal with the matter himself, or report it to his -- the offender's superior officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he has that discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not an ideal time to pause, but there will not be one in the next few minutes. So I think we might as well take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will take the break first, and we will resume at 25 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, I have been advised very gently by the interpreters that I am not making a pause and that I am speaking too quickly. If I could please have your assistance in helping me by making a pause yourself, I will be grateful, and the interpreters, surely, will be as well.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will it my best. I am aware of my own failings of talking too fast, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Before the break, we were discussing Article 26 of the Code of Military Discipline, you will recall.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to stay -- actually, before that, in your review of the evidence or of all the documents you have reviewed, did you see any disciplinary issued by General Cermak to anyone or him referring any breaches of military discipline to anyone?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we stay with Article 26 but now look at the next paragraph, it states that the officers under paragraph 1, which you will remember included garrison commanders, shall issue disciplinary measures within the powers prescribed by Article 22. If we now go to Article 22, which starts --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 23 it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. 23. Which is two pages prior. And I will go through a number of Articles and then ask you a question at the end. So if I am moving too fast at any stage, just let me know and we will take it in turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So we start at the bottom of the page, Article 23. Just focus on that a little bit for everyone else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we see the powers described in Articles 21 and 22, which we'll get to next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we turn the page to item 4 in the English, to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We see that the powers of a major-general or higher is given the authority of a corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to know what that mean, let's go to the page before again, to Article 22. And this states: "The commander of a brigade or corps or more senior commanders shall be empowered to pronounce all disciplinary measures prescribed under this Code." And now these measures are listed in Article 10, which this time now we have to go to page 5 to look at Article 10. And we see that those measures include -- go up to detention for up to 30 days. And this applies to all servicemen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could just briefly go back to Article 22, which was on page 8, the second sentence of Article 22:

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "These officers shall decide the responsibility of soldiers, guardsmen, reserve soldiers, and cadets for the offences specified in paragraph 1, Article 12, of this Code." And just to be completely clear, this refers to commanders of a brigade, corps, or more senior; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And finally, hopefully the last time we jump around, if we do go to the Article that is referenced, paragraph -- Article 12, paragraph 1, which details specifically with soldiers, guardsmen, reserve soldiers, and cadets, and they may be able to get up to a sentence of up to 60 days in custody if no other disciplinary measures under Article 10 corresponds to the gravity of the offence." Now, General, I know we've gone through these very quick now, so if you want to look back at any of them, just let me know and we will do so. But if we put all these Articles together, 10, 12, 22, 23, and 26, we have a situation where a garrison commander with the rank of a colonel-general could issue disciplinary measures of up to 30 days' detention to all servicemen. And with respect to soldiers, if the gravity of the offence was such that it was not sufficient, he could issue a disciplinary measure of up to 60 days' detention. Is that an accurate summary of the provision we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the emphasis on a disciplinary measure which has to be for a minor violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one of the changes you made in your corrigendum, it was change number 10, and it referred to -- I'll just find it for you, the exact page reference. It is page 31, line 14. It's actually 34, line 14. I was misled by the corrigendum which was still a matter to resolve with the page differences. And I've talked to Mr. Cayley and it's -- the wrong version was uploaded which was the problem. And I have been assured that the right one will be uploaded, then there will be no problems. You've changed -- so you were saying here that his powers, talking about General Cermak, of punishment were determined by his rank. And under Articles 22 and 23, he was authorised to award a range of punishments from a caution to 30 days' detention. And you initially had 60 days which we just saw would apply to soldiers if Article 10 was not appropriate. Can you tell us what made you change that 60 days, which I think is correct, to the 30 which is only within Article 10?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I was advised that I was wrong in law in my interpretation of the military law to say 60 days, and I'm, you know, I'm not a lawyer. I'm not a military lawyer. I'm a practitioner of military law; and I'm not even a practitioner of Croatian military law. And in order to ensure that I did not put something in the report which was not in line with the law, I changed it. But I also felt that the difference between 30 and 60, particularly when dealing with minor violations, was of no great importance because, in fact, what we see in terms of the sort of generic crimes that were being committed, in this particular case, then, in my judgement, they were not minor violations, they were actually major violations. So to me it was a technical issue. It didn't really change -- it certainly change my -- my view, my judgement of -- of -- of how I saw the law affecting -- the law being effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Who advised you that you were wrong in law and caused you to make that change?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the Cermak Defence team. As a result of, you know, the -- when I sent my report in, it was one of the comments that I had made an error in my -- my view of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I thought you had stated earlier that everything you had in your report was your own conclusions. Your own conclusion seemed to be 60 days. And I appreciate it's not a major matter, but your own conclusion was 60 days. Then you were told that was wrong and to change it to 30 days, and you did so.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- when I was giving you my -- my statement that everything in the -- in the -- my report was my own view, I was talking about my opinion, my judgement. Quite clearly, if I -- if I made a mistake, a factual mistake, there was little point in me maintaining that factual mistake because it was my, you know, that is what I had decided. If it was, indeed, a factual mistake. And I was unable to, you know, I did not debate it very strongly. Deferred to those who knew the law better than I did, and I changed it. As I say, it didn't seem to me to be a very important issue, because it was dealing with minor violations. When, in fact, the focus of the case is on very -- on -- on major violations and serious criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to be clear, that -- that change was between that first report that you sent that we discussed and this version of the report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this's true, yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you advised of any other mistakes or inaccuracies that you should change in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In between my -- my report and my -- the report that has been tabled, yes, and they're largely covered in the corrigendum. Those are the mistakes and inaccuracies which were identified, some of them -- most of them in terms of footnotes, because I'm a computer illiterate, I'm afraid, and I failed to master the system particularly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So does that mean that all the changes in your corrigendum came from the Cermak Defence team, who asked you to make those changes and then you -- those are the ones that are reflected?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes they were. Apart from one, which I will -- I'm happy to talk about. Which is on -- which is number 7 and 8. But all the rest came from comments which had been made when my report had been looked at, because there were errors in it. I mean, now -- if I may, Your Honour, talk about number 7 and 8. Page 30, line 3 and 4, reads or should now read: "Equipment to meet the pressing demands that existed, Particular," et cetera, et cetera. And then at line 8 should read: "Vehicles to assist in the normalisation of the Knin area." I had used the word "task" in there. And when I was reading the report myself, I realised that it was a rather casual use of the word. It's a term of speech that I use myself. A task is something I give myself; a task is something I have to do. But I realised that I used it in a context there which implied that this was task given to General Cermak by somebody else. And that was not what I meant. And, therefore, I changed it to the words you have there. That was done entirely by my own accord. That was not a comment made by the Cermak Defence team. It was a change that I made, in order, I hope, to clarify what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Are you done with your comment on --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- number 7 and 8?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. That is the end of my comment. That is merely for transparency and clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just wanted to give you an opportunity to say what you wanted to say. There's another -- well, maybe we'll deal with it later and go back to the Code of Military Discipline. And you said, before we got sidetracked, but it was largely my fault. Let me just find it so that I quote your exact words. I asked you, and that's at page 142, lines 13 to 20. I asked you: "If we put all these Articles together, 10, 12, 22, 23, and 26, we have a situation where a garrison commander with the rank of a colonel-general could issue up to 30 days' detention to all servicemen. And with respect to soldiers, if the gravity of the offence was not sufficient, he could issue a disciplinary measure of up to 60 days' detention." And I asked you: "Is that an accurate summary of the provisions we looked at?" And your answer was: "Yes. And the emphasise on a disciplinary measure which has to be for minor violation." Now, Article 12 expressly deals with criminal offences; correct? I think you have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And those would not be a minor violation, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those, in my view, are not a minor violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your report, I'm talking about page 33, lines 38, and spilling over to the next page, you state that: "It is the authorised prosecutor who has the responsibility and authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings." If we look at Article 31 - that is at page 10 in the English, at the bottom - now, this deals with a situation where an offence is both against military discipline and also a criminal offence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says: "In situations where the authorised officer finds that the offence against military discipline is also a criminal offence, the case shall be sent via regular channels to the authorised prosecutor. If he thinks that it is in the interest of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary procedures." Now, you interpret the "he" in the second part of the sentence to be the authorised prosecutor, not the authorised officer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Read the whole thing, yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, I think that is actually quite ambiguous - isn't it? - because it could refer to either the authorised officer or the authorised prosecutor, and I, frankly, from that small paragraph, I couldn't tell which it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just as a matter of military doctrine, since we're referring to something that is both a criminal offence and a disciplinary offence, would it make sense that the disciplinary procedure would be initiated by the authorised officer and the criminal proceeding by the authorise the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- in -- in most -- in most systems, certainly the one that I'm in, if there is a serious criminal offence, this becomes immediately a matter for the civil police. If the military police are involved at all, it is in -- it is to assist them. If you're talking about here, which you are, an offence against military discipline, and we see this with the military police sending through Major Juric to the Split military prosecutor's office the details of crimes committed which were being investigated. And they went straight through up the criminal chain of the military police, which was part of the military police administration responsibility, that went straight through the criminal chain to the Split Military District prosecutor. Who, then, decides to initiate disciplinary procedures, which, after all, is a discretion, because it only has to be done if people believe it is in the interests of the service. And it is my judgement and my experience that this is normally administrative action to remove somebody from the army who is -- who is -- committed an a criminal offence. So that instead of the person receiving his criminal punishment or her criminal punishment and then coming back into army, because you may not wish them to serve on, you make administrative action against them. And that my -- that is one interpretation of this particular paragraph. So I don't think it -- to me it doesn't particularly matter who that "he" refers to, because both of those he's, so to speak, can exercise their judgement in the interests of the service and actually, therefore, initiate disciplinary procedures, whatever they may be. Of course, we -- we should -- I should repeat that the authorised officer is only authorised to deal with those soldiers under his command who are subordinated, and with Mr. Cermak, that was very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, I will not start the argument with you over again on Article 26. I think our position is clear and your position is clear, and I don't want to repeat it over and over again about who an authorised officer was. But I'm interested in -- there is nothing that excludes both a criminal proceeding and a parallel disciplinary procedure in the case of a violation of military discipline. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a view as to whether it is in the interests of the service so to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Both can proceed at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm seeking the Court's guidance here, and I can say that in front of the witness, Article 31, I was told that there may be a -- not a -- translation issue as to the interpretation of that word "he" in that some words may be in the Croatian language and, of course, I don't speak Croatian, but some words in the Croatian language, if they would refer to the -- to the last reference, would include some other words. Since it is an admitted exhibit, I don't know how to proceed. We can send a request for clarification. But I am seeking the Court's guidance just so that we can have the right -- I think the witness has answered to the best of his ability, and that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To what the "he" refers seems not to be resolved in the English language clearly. Some ambiguity remains. Now, whether that's different in the original language can be explored. But then I think that a very precise question has to be put to CLSS, that is, that whether, from a linguistic point of view, that there is a preference for to whom the "he" refers. And if, linguistically, there would be a preference, what then exactly defines that preference? That may be a question that can be submitted to CLSS, but I'm looking at the parties to see whether any better suggestion --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The only reason I'm asking, I know there have been some changes in the procedure for admitted exhibits, and I don't know if it has to go through the Registrar or from the parties. And that's simply in terms of a focussed question on an exhibit that is already admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... yes, and, of course, only the linguistical aspect could be covered by such a question. Well, how to do it exactly, to whom to send it, and who to give approval of such an exercise is -- I have no answer to you right away. But I'm seeking the assistance of the parties on the type of question that could be put to CLSS and whether the way in which I phrased it would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- it might be helpful to know what the Prosecution thinks is missing or not correct and then we could determine whether -- how to phrase the specific question, but at this point, we're not sure what the exact issue is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the exact issue is - but please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Hedaraly - whether in the original language the same ambiguity would be there. That is, ambiguity as to whom the "he" refers. That seems to be the issue. And sometimes it may not be possible to translate it but to give some further explanation as to the linguistic context of this translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it would help if Mr. Hedaraly and I talked at the end of the session, because I'm not sure if we're just simply asking for an updated translation or are we asking CLSS to provide an opinion on -- on the text, in which case I would like to, at least, know specifically the Prosecution is positing as the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to formulate it, but apparently you -- let me keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you discuss the matter with Mr. Hedaraly before any request will be sent to anyone, this Chamber is still confident that it certainly would assist, whatever the result will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But talking never harms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just so that we're absolutely clear, General, you don't speak Croatian, do you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You have already referred in your report to Article 69 of the Code which is at page 19. I won't go through it in detail but simply pointing out that General Cermak did not have the authority to bring charges to a military disciplinary court, as this is limited to the commanders of an operation -- of operational zones. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We're in agreement on that. I wanted to draw your attention to Article 66, which is on the previous page, which says that: "An officer who initiated an investigation can send the case to an officer authorised to bring charges before a military disciplinary court if he himself is not authorised to do so." Now, I know and I think it is clear to everyone that your position is that a garrison commander is not authorised to initiate such an investigation for people that are not his direct subordinates. But you will agree with me that officers unable to bring these charges can send the case to an officer who is able to bring those charges. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to me to be what that Article means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 33 -- if we return to page 33 of your report --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Pardon me. You state that the allegation reported by the internationals were clearly criminal offences, and, as such, are matters for the civil police over which Cermak had no authority. And when you say General Cermak had no authority over the civilian police, you are referring to the fact that garrison commanders typically don't have authority over the civilian police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do not, according to the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in your report, at page 36 this time, line 33, when discussing these crimes, you stated that: "These acts were thought by the Croatian authorities to be carried out by members of the Home Guard and HV who originally came from the area. Some were also thought to be civilians wearing military clothing." When criminal offences are perpetrated or appear to be perpetrated by military persons, then it's not the civilian police but the military police who would deal with the matter; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my experience. When serious criminal offences are committed by soldiers, and everything I read in there inclined me to believe that the same principle applied, not least because the level of punishment would have been quite clearly inadequate and not least because we keep going back to issue that General Cermak in particular could only deal with a -- minor violations. This would have immediately, in my judgement, and I think it's reasonable to suppose, would have been a police, a civil police matter. Now, it may be that the military reported it to the civil police and identified the nature of the crime, the place, and the time, because, I would suggest that for any investigation to -- to be instigated, at least all those factors have to be -- have some sort of -- of content. It may be a rather general content or may be very specific, you know, it happened at, where, and what. But there has to be some -- some specifics there. Otherwise, it is very difficult to see how somebody can investigate a general statement that crimes were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I may have been unclear in my question. In a specific example of a soldier being -- being seen committing a criminal offence, if it is established that that person is a soldier, would it still be a matter for the civilian police to deal with or would it be a matter for the military police to deal with?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- can you, please, define what you mean by "deal with." Investigate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, let's start with investigate.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigate. Well, I believe that if the crime is serious enough - and you've used the word "criminal offence" - I believe that that immediately becomes something which the civilian police should be responsible for, would be responsible for. Maybe it is reported to them by the military police, but they then conduct the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to a slightly different topic yet not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can have D1667 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this just goes back to the issue of the authority of General Cermak, just so you know. Or, rather, as you will see the --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- the authority that he may have suggested he had. I know you dealt with this briefly earlier today, and I just want to ask you a few more questions on that. These are the notes, the notebook of a man who was at that initial meeting with General Cermak on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 40 of those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to show you a portion which is -- you saw the sitrep from the following day. This is the actual minutes. You see at the middle of the page, there, it says -- the handwriting is sometimes messy, though. I will read out what I understand this to mean, and my learned friends will -- if they take issue with it, they will surely intervene. But we've been through it before, so it should be okay. You see in the middle, there, it says: "Brigadier General Forand want freedom of movement total and not have it disappear after Special Representative of Secretary-General leaves." And General Cermak responds: "... what," -- I think the parties will agree is Gotovina, "... to see what areas are safe for freedom of movement from tomorrow, should be able to move in most of my area of responsibility, including in Knin town. If you have any problems ... see me personally." And there's a similar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we could just get the right page and the B/C/S so the clients can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I didn't know whether the translation might check, so I didn't look at it. I apologise. But it should be a few pages, because the -- it should be the next page because we see the ERN on the top with 6917. In the bottom of the B/C/S, now, is 6915, so to the next page in the B/C/S. In the middle there, 6917, should be the right portion in the middle, Forand and then Cermak. And I will just pause for a few seconds so that everyone in the courtroom can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, in your report at page 53, you refer to another similar report from the UN. This one was dated 24th of August. It's P374. There's no need to bring it up on the screen, unless you want to. You will see from my question to be -- not be necessary. Where, essentially, once again, General Cermak referred to his area of responsibility. And you commented that: "It is difficult to ascertain whether this was a general statement of the difficulties of preventing such events in a large and rugged area or whether General Cermak genuinely felt it was his area of responsibilities. If he did, then he misunderstood his actual authority, and in doing so, misled probably unwittingly UNCRO?"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just for clarity, my learned friend missed out the word responsibility from that sentence, just for accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I apologise if I did. I wasn't -- it wasn't meant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry could you just give me the lines again. I have lost my --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was page 53 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- of your report, at the very top. It's just this issue of General Cermak perhaps saying this was an issue -- his area of responsibility. And then you suggested that he perhaps unwittingly made those comments. That's the general issue that I want to ask you a question about.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, if we accept that General Cermak made those statements on the 7th of August, on the 24th of August, that that was his area of responsibility, and if we also accept your opinion that General Cermak did not actually have this authority that he claimed, that leaves two options, right? Either General Cermak was unaware that he did not have this authority; or he was aware of it and deliberately misrepresented his authority; correct? Those are the two options?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the two options, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if it's the former, if it's that General Cermak was unaware that he had this authority, he was acting as if he did have it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now move to the issue of the appointment of Major Jonjic which is a series of documents addressed in your report. And as soon as I locate the right page, I will direct you to it. It's page 40 of your report, lines 20 to 27. And there is a series of three documents. And, just very briefly, that was the order by General Cermak to assign Major Jonjic to the Knin garrison. And you remember that issue?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to go through these documents in a little more detail than you have in your report. So if we start with the first one chronologically which is D759. This is General Cermak's order of the 9th of August. Here it is. And at item one of the order, he orders Major Jonjic to be assign temporarily to the garrison, the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And item two, he orders the logistics base of the Sibenik sector commander to issue an order appointing his temporary replacement, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your opinion, in your report, about this order, was that by General Cermak, and I'll quote "overstepped the mark" with this order, right? That was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And as support for this, you referred to the response of the logistics base commander?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So let's have that on screen, which is going to be D758. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says that: "Due to Major Jonjic leaving the duty of his own will and making himself available to the Knin garrison and that the order of the Knin garrison commander" -- and there's a reference to the orders which is seen, "... the system of command ... has been seriously affected [sic]." Now, obviously, from this language, we can see that Major Pavic iis not to pleased with loosing Major Jonjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, despite this, he still orders a replacement as he was ordered to do by General Cermak in D759; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it is also clear from Major Pavic's order that he is complaining more about Major Jonjic's behaviour, as we can see from item two in a possible disciplinary procedure, and nowhere in this order is there a suggestion that General Cermak could not issue this order to him, is there?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh. I think you're -- you're reading an enormous amount into this order, I'm afraid. I would regard, I mean, can I see why you should do so, but I think this order very clearly identifies that General Cermak had no authority to issue that order. We know he had no authority to issue that order because the logistic base was not under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Please, sir -- I understand your position. I want to focus on this document you've said that I'm reading a lot into it. So are you. And I'm asking you, in this order, you said, This order -- not talking about his authority that we know or don't know that he has. You say, This order very clearly identifies that General Cermak had no authority to issue that order. What I am putting to you is that it does not say that. I mean, in fact, the person who received it did what General Cermak told him to do which is appoint a replacement.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, he did, because he to appoint a replacement legally. I would suggest -- when I use the word "legally," I would suggest that if you have a commander who absents himself, as he technically did, because he was not given permission to go to work for General Cermak, then the overall commander has a responsibility to place in that particular absent post, that empty post, somebody with the legal authority to continue the work of the base. Otherwise, the base has no command structure. I don't think he was -- I would suggest that he was not -- as it were, obeying an order, but obeying a necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I accept that as being your position. Can you identify for me where it very clearly indicates that Major Pavic is of the view that General Cermak did not have the authority to issue him that order?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't state it in there. And the word "indication" I'm using because I get from the -- this letter that Major Pavic is saying to General Cermak, You shouldn't have done that. Is quite difficult, as a major, to write an angry letter to a General, even though that general may not have the military background or indeed the authority of other generals. So there is a dynamic here between very substantially different ranks. And he also sends, you will notice, to General Gotovina. So it's quite clear that Major Pavic is happy to raise this as a complaint with General Gotovina. And I think that's what he has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what I'm suggesting to you that in item two, he was also upset at Major Jonjic's behaviour; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's look at the final document of that series, which is D760, which is General Cermak's response. And this is a General Cermak's response which you've described in your report as being an angry response. And if you look at that, I will suggest to you that General Cermak's anger, as you have described it, is directed at the unnecessary insinuations that is stated, or perhaps threatened, disciplinary procedures against Major Jonjic. And I will further suggest to you, sir, that contrary to what you conclude, this, in fact, shows the authority of General Cermak to issue orders to at least the 306th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may make that judgement which I can understand how you draw those conclusions. I think it is reasonable to draw the conclusion from the clearly stated authority, as laid down in the regulations, as to what General Cermak's authority was, in terms of who he -- who was subordinated to him, and his -- his authority to subordinate other people to him or other units to him and that was extremely limited. What he does here is get cross with Major Pavic for coming back to him in the way he did. And I think what we see here is an argument between two men, two commanders, over an order which was given, in my judgement, and I think I'm trying to be -- to look at this in a reasonable way, and I think it was clear that -- in my reading of the regulations, that General Cermak did not have the authority to do it. And I think we, there, see an example of what happens, the sort of breakdown in communications, when people fail to appreciate the limits of their authority. And I believe that this was about General Cermak not understanding the system. He had only been in the garrison a few days. He had no -- none of the previous experience that a soldier would have had. How was he to know how these things were done? And I believe you will see from documents in the future that he begins to learn after a time there are ways of doing things in the military, in terms of asking your superior commander if he will authorise a transfer of soldiers from A to B in order to support you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we will get to those. Let me ask you this: In the documents that you reviewed, did you see any disciplinary procedures against Major Jonjic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we go to P2525, at page 67, which is the interview that General Cermak gave in 2001 to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: For some reason, there is not a translation link to that document. I will try to look into it. I apologise in the meantime. I will try to read slowly the short portion I'm referring to for the benefit of those listening in B/C/S. If we go to the bottom of that page, General Cermak says: "We arrived in the morning in Sibenik, and we went to the logistics base. We got in touch with Major Jonjic." This is on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "I told him, I needed the right men and right team of logistics people for Knin and that I needed his help to see what men we can have in the beginning of [sic] the afternoon I boarded the helicopter and left for Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I read "what men we can have in the beginning and in the afternoon." So not the beginning "of" the afternoon, but in the afternoon he boarded the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I must have written it down wrong, I was going through my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's almost the same but not entirely. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then there's a further exchange from line 1 to 7 which relates, more or less, similar issues. And line 8 is what I want to focus on. The question is: "No. So yourself and Major Jonjic decided between you, what you needed, and you set in train a system to arrange for these people to be made available?" General Cermak responds: "We didn't decide what to do. I told him what I needed, I needed some people for Knin, to set off for Knin and do all of that."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You had not seen that when discussing the orders regarding Major Jonjic, had you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, I will ask you a similar question to what I asked you before. If General Cermak was unaware of his authority, he was acting as if he did have that authority - right? - by issuing these orders and telling people what to do?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was meeting a demand which he had been given. I get concerned when you represent it by saying he acted "as if he had the authority." We go back to the direction from the President, Go down and sort out Knin and help the Canadians. General Cermak, essentially, is a patriot. He is a man who wished to serve his country, and I think it's important that we understand that. Furthermore, he was businessman. And businessmen are not supported by staff. Unlike the military, they are not so bound in hierarchy and process and procedure, because business is very different from conducting complex operations where you have to have these very, at times, as I have said in my report, at times, Bizantine rules, and regulations. And I think what we see here - and, again, this is my judgement, my interpretation, which is all I can do, and I hope it is a reasonable interpretation. All we see here is major -- I'm sorry, General Cermak attempting to solve the problem he believes he has. Unfortunately, he does so in a way which actually runs across, runs counter to the process and procedures of -- of subordination and superiority, and he finds that it is very difficult, until he learns later on how to do it. And then it becomes, actually, really very simple for him. And I believe that's what you're seeing here. That is my judgement. That is how I read the evidence that I both saw myself and that I now see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So that's on the 6th. If you look at line 4 on the top of the screen: "When I arrived in Sibenik, I told Major Jonjic and later we got the paperwork in order regarding the transfer." And we know the orders was issued on the 9th of August; correct? And what I'm suggesting to you is that when General Cermak issued that order to Major Jonjic, he thought that was something that he could do, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would agree that he thought he could do it. Otherwise, he wouldn't have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the following paragraph of your report, it's page 40, starting at line 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you dealt with this subject or -- Mr. Hedaraly, or are you still --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have dealt with the issue of Major Jonjic. I'm going to go on to the orders regarding other members to be transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would not mind, I would ask one or two questions in relation to this. And that is in order, since we are talking about it now, it is better done immediately. I noticed that in the three documents we saw, the first one, 9th of August, second one, 11th of August, third one, 16th of August. Now, in the first one, General Cermak appoints Mr. Jonjic and orders his replacement in the Sibenik Logistics Base. Now, in the second document - and I'm specifically asking your attention for that - apparently Mr. Pavic is unhappy. He says, Jonjic voluntarily left. And then he says, Due to this, and at the order of. So he gives two reasons. The first one being that well, that he left and he apparently takes the position that wherever he may have been appointed, he was never discharged of his duties here. But he adds, then, as a second reason, And at the order of. And then, among other matters, he replaces. When asked about this matter by Mr. Hedaraly, you said, Well, of course, what could he else do than to replace this vacancy -- this person who had left? Now, my question to you is - and we are interpreting, to some extent, text as well - could he have said, Well, due to the situation that Jonjic is gone, I have to replace because there's no one there in his place anymore. But he specifically uses the language "at the order of." Now, does that mean anything as far as acceptance of such an order, because we've said quite a bit about whether Mr. Cermak was unaware of his authority, but the language "at the order of," suggests that Mr. Pavic, at least, had that impression or didn't want to deny such an authority. Could you help me out how to understand exactly this "at the order of," in addition to the actual situation that existed since Jonjic had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I will try. Could I have it on my screen, please, so I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's D758.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the -- oh, thank you. I've just got the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it takes a moment to have the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I was primarily focussing on the first paragraph: "Due to ..." up to the word "order."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, this is extremely complicated and very nuanced, and, you see, I think I could read that -- that because he says - and I hope we don't get into detailed argument about -- about the use of words here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I won't be in argument with you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, sir, I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... never are, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I don't intend to get in argument with you, Your Honour, either. I think I might know who comes off worst. He says at the order of -- well, I'll read -- if I may, I'll read it from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do it slowly for our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "Due to the commander of Sibenik Department 306th Logistics Base Split," I'll -- "Major ... Jonjic, leaving of the duty on his own will and making himself available to the Knin garrison commander, and at the order of the Knin garrison commander ..." and then a string of letters "... by which the system of command has been seriously disrupted." I believe that that refers not to "at the order of the Knin garrison commander, I hereby order ..." I believe that is his way of saying that he left duty of his own will and at the order of the Knin garrison commander. That is it the way I would interpret it. I would also suggest that -- that there is an another issue here, the -- the Croatian Army was, like many armies, very procedural. And we see that all the orders, many -- most of the orders, follow a very particular pattern. And -- and I think we may be seeing part of that here, that it is written as an order, because that is the only way he could write it, even though he might have said, I appoint, merely rather than saying, I order. Now would that have been different? I don't know. But it would not have used the word "order." But I -- to go back to the main point, I read that that the phrase "at the order of Knin garrison commander" is linked to Jonjic's leaving his duty of his own will, on his own will, rather than at the order of the Knin garrison commander, "I hereby order." Now, whether that is a correct interpretation, sir, or not, you must decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will. If there's need to do so. But just -- my question, linguistically, reading due to this circumstance and at the order of the Knin garrison commander I hereby order, could that be - and I'm not a native speaking person - could that also mean that the order is given at the order previously mentioned. Whether that's the correct interpretation, but I'm purely asking you linguistically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could mean -- to me, it could mean both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both. Thank you for that answer. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note the time. There is an series of two or three documents that I wanted to address in the same way. I, therefore, don't want to start and have it interrupted, if we need the series of documents. And I think the 6.00 time was quite a firm one, so I think, in these circumstances, maybe it's time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it depends on -- and that's the last thing I wanted to inquire about where you are. Tomorrow, as you know, we start at 11.00 only, and we would have Wednesday. Are you confident or would be your assessment as to the moment in which you think could you conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's hard to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have skipped around a little bit. I am definitely sure that we don't need the Chamber to consider 15 bis tomorrow. That's already been stated and that -- nothing can change that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... yes, but that depends Mr. Hedaraly, also, of the Defence. So could you give us an indication as to when you think you would -- would that be tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First session, second session, third session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think I will be able to complete tomorrow. It's very difficult to give an exact estimate, but I'm hopeful that, at the very least, by the end of tomorrow, I will be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would then have Wednesday morning, and one session in the afternoon available. I'm addressing the Defence. Mr. Cayley, would that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that would be plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Misetic and -- Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that would be enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, under those circumstances, we will adjourn for the day. Mr. Deverell, I would like to instruct you, as I did before, not to speak with anyone about your testimony, either already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow, Tuesday, the 10th of November, at 11.00 in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of November, 2009, at 11.00 a.m.
